title: A Fast Algorithm to Simulate Nonlinear Resistive Networks
authors: Benjamin Scellier (sole author)
venue: ICML 2024, PMLR 235 (Vienna); arXiv v1 Feb 2024, v2 6 Jun 2024
claim: Treats the steady state of ideal nonlinear resistive networks (conductances plus diodes, Kirchhoff energy) as a quadratic program with linear inequality constraints and solves it exactly by block coordinate descent on a GPU. Compared with SPICE-based EP (Kendall et al. 2020: 0.16M weights, 3.43% MNIST error, about 1 week), it trains deep resistive networks 327x larger (51.7M weights) and 160x faster. MNIST test error: EP 1.33% vs BP 1.30% (XL), EP 3.46% vs BP 3.30% (XS). Code is at github.com/rain-neuromorphics/energy-based-learning; the newest commit in the feed is 2025-04-06.
check: Full text (pdftotext of v2) supports every number and method detail. Steady state of ideal networks is a "convex quadratic programming (QP) problem with linear inequality constraints", solved by exact coordinate descent, and by exact block coordinate descent for layered DRNs. Quote: "327 times as many parameters as the DRN-XS architecture used in Kendall et al. (2020) (51.7M vs 0.16M)". Table 1: SPICE XS 3.43%, 1 week. XS EP 3.46±0.07 vs BP 3.30±0.13. XL EP 1.33±0.02 vs BP 1.30±0.03. Code link github.com/rain-neuromorphics/energy-based-learning is confirmed, and its commits.atom shows the newest commit at 2025-04-06.
relevance: This is the best ready-made emulator of a physical learning machine for our MLP/MNIST line. We could run EP or coupled learning on it and apply hub-allocation pruning to the conductances. Two limits: EP matching BP in this emulator is already shown, so 'a local rule matches BP' would not be new; and the simulator is ideal (no device variation, noise or drift) with no energy or time model. We would have to add the scoreboard ourselves as a model-based estimate (dissipated power sum G*dV^2, relaxation time, update energy). It only supports layered MLP-like networks, so CNN/CIFAR class-incremental runs are not directly possible.

title: Unsupervised and probabilistic learning with Contrastive Local Learning Networks: The Restricted Kirchhoff Machine
authors: Marcelo Guzman, Simone Ciarella, Andrea J. Liu
claim: Proposes a self-learning resistor network built on the twin-network CLLN technology that runs an RBM-like contrastive local rule. Simulated training on binarized MNIST performs comparably to RBMs. The paper derives how time, power and energy per operation scale (node relaxation, ADC, gate-voltage updates) and compares this with RBM matrix-vector products measured on a CPU and GPU (i7-13700H, RTX 4050). RKM energy grows linearly with the number of hidden units, while CPU/GPU matmul approaches quadratic growth. The stated training advantage is a factor of 1/Nh at fixed Nv.
check: Full text supports every point. The paper says: "scaling of time, power, and energy consumption for training is better than for RBMs on centralized platforms by a factor of 1/Nh, when ... Nv is kept fixed." Fig. 6 uses torch.matmul on "an Intel i7-13700H and an NVIDIA 4050 GPU". RKM energy "increases linearly with Nh", while CPU/GPU matmul "approaches a quadratic scaling". The training is a simulation on binarized MNIST with Nh=500. Classification peaks around 92%, which is comparable to an RBM trained under the same conditions.
relevance: This is a direct precedent for rescoring on the machine's own costs for CLLNs. It shows such a scoreboard is publishable, but it is a scaling argument against GPU matmul, not end-to-end energy at equal accuracy. A stronger version (our candidate) would fix accuracy, count the twin-network overhead and I/O, and compare against memory-saving BP. That fits our rule that energy is a model-based estimate only.

title: Energy-Based Learning Algorithms for Analog Computing: A Comparative Study
authors: Benjamin Scellier, Maxence Ernoult, Jack Kendall, Suhas Kumar (Rain AI)
venue: NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems); arXiv v1 22 Dec 2023
claim: Compares 7 energy-based rules (contrastive learning, and EP and coupled learning each with positive, negative or centered nudging) on deep convolutional Hopfield networks in GPU simulation. CIFAR-10 test error: centered EP 11.1%, negative EP 11.9%, centered CpL 14.9%, positive CpL 46.9%, CL 31.4%, against truncated BP 10.1% and recurrent BP 10.7%. CIFAR-100: C-EP 37.0%, C-CpL 46.5%, TBP 33.4%. Negative and centered nudging beat positive nudging. A 300-epoch C-EP run reaches 9.70% on CIFAR-10. Asynchronous updates plus 16-bit precision give a 13.5x speed-up.
check: All numbers match Table 1 (mean of 3 runs, test error %): CIFAR-10 TBP 10.1, RBP 10.7, CL 31.4, N-EP 11.9, C-EP 11.1, P-CpL 46.9, C-CpL 14.9; CIFAR-100 TBP 33.4, C-EP 37.0, C-CpL 46.5. Abstract: "negative perturbations are better than positive ones, and highlight the centered variant of EP ... as the best-performing algorithm." Table 2: C-EP 300 epochs gives 9.70% on CIFAR-10. Abstract: "13.5 times faster with respect to Laborieux et al. [2021] ... asynchronous updates, combined with reduced precision (16 bits)." Setup: deep convolutional Hopfield networks (DCHNs) on five vision tasks (MNIST, F-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100), simulated on GPU.
relevance: Shows which local contrastive rule to emulate and what accuracy to expect. Coupled learning, the rule built into CLLN hardware, falls behind EP and BP as tasks get harder, so an emulator study must report CpL and EP separately. Even the best rule stays about 1 point behind BP on CIFAR-10 and about 4 points on CIFAR-100. The largest EP-family result in simulation is ImageNet 32x32 matching BP (holomorphic EP, NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2209.00530); no physical hardware is near that scale.

title: Understanding and Embracing Imperfection in Physical Learning Networks
authors: Dillavou, Sam; Guzman, Marcelo; Liu, Andrea J.; Durian, Douglas J.
venue: arXiv preprint (v1 28 May 2025, v2 17 Mar 2026; no journal-ref on the abs page)
claim: Trains a real transistor-based contrastive local learning network (twin networks, coupled-learning rule) on two tasks in alternation. It shows limit cycles and error scaling with the switching period that are absent in 'perfect' simulations. Training longer on one task erases the other. The cause is an uncontrolled learning bias in measurement and update, which the authors liken to representational drift. An analytic model reproduces this, and a system-agnostic 'overclamping' protocol largely suppresses it and improves classification.
check: Abstract: "observe limit cycles and scaling behaviors that limit precision, erase memory of previous tasks, and are absent in `perfect' systems ... reminiscent of representational drift in the brain." The full text confirms the rest. It is a MOSFET-edge CLLN with twin Free/Clamped networks and the Coupled Learning rule. Two tasks are trained alternately with period tau; error is flat for short and long tau and rises monotonically in between. An analytic biased-update model has no free parameters. The paper also introduces "overclamping".
relevance: Counter-evidence for our online class-incremental setting. On real physical learners, forgetting can come from device bias rather than gradient interference, and an ideal emulator (such as Scellier's) would not show it. A positive emulator result should include bias and offset models in the update rule and test the overclamping fix; otherwise it is optimistic.

title: Physical learning beyond the quasistatic limit
authors: Stern, M., Dillavou, S., Miskin, M. Z., Durian, D. J., Liu, A. J.
venue: arXiv Dec 2021 (cond-mat.dis-nn); published Phys. Rev. Research 4, L022037 (2022)
claim: Runs coupled learning in an electrical resistor network, in the lab and on the computer, at learning rates from slow to far above the physical relaxation rate. Up to a critical ratio of learning rate to relaxation rate, learning speeds up with little change in behaviour or error. Beyond that threshold the error oscillates, but the network still learns.
check: Abstract: "up to a critical threshold in the ratio of the learning rate to the physical rate of relaxation, learning speeds up without much change of behavior or error. Beyond the critical threshold, the error exhibits oscillatory dynamics but the networks still learn successfully." Lab network uses capacitors (2.2-2200 uF) to slow relaxation; simulations on N=64 networks agree. Claim matches.
relevance: Supports the 'learning and inference at the same time' principle and gives an emulator setting that GPUs lack: wall-clock time per update is set by physical relaxation, and learning need not wait for equilibrium. Related work shows that desynchronized per-edge updates do not hurt in simulation and help in experiment (Wycoff et al., J. Chem. Phys. 156, 144903, 2022; arXiv:2201.04626). On our scoreboard, time-to-accuracy should be counted in relaxation times while sweeping the learning/relaxation ratio.

title: Machine learning without a processor: Emergent learning in a nonlinear analog network (PNAS title; arXiv v2 title: "Machine Learning Without a Processor: Emergent Learning in a Nonlinear Electronic Metamaterial")
authors: Dillavou, S., Beyer, B. D., Stern, M., Liu, A. J., Miskin, M. Z., Durian, D. J.
venue: arXiv preprint 1 Nov 2023 (v2 5 Apr 2024); published PNAS 121(28), e2319718121 (2024)
claim: Builds a clockless analog twin network of self-adjusting nonlinear resistors made from transistors that implements the exact coupled-learning rule. Without a computer it learns XOR and nonlinear regression, which linear networks cannot do. It retrains in seconds and performs tasks in microseconds. Training error falls mode by mode (mean, then slope, then curvature), like spectral bias. The appendix reports inference power of 151 uW for XOR and 345+/-72 uW across 29 tasks, about 5-10 uW per edge, or about 10-20 pJ per edge assuming 2 us.
check: Supported by the full text. Abstract: "learns tasks unachievable in linear systems, including XOR and nonlinear regression, without a computer ... reduces modes of training error in order (mean, slope, curvature)". Appendix: "For the XOR task ... 151 uW. For the 29 tasks ... 345+/-72 uW ... approximately 5 or 10 uW per edge", and "assuming 2 uS ... 10 or 20 pJ of dissipation per edge". The paper also states it "implements the full (not approximate) Coupled Learning rule", with retraining in seconds and inference in microseconds.
relevance: Gives device-level numbers we can use to parameterize a CLLN cost model, and an example of learning while operating: the free network keeps computing while the clamped twin supplies the contrast. The tasks are toy-sized; CLLN hardware has reached only XOR, iris and regression. Any CIFAR-scale claim on this machine would be an emulator-only extrapolation and should be labeled as such.

title: Demonstration of Decentralized Physics-Driven Learning (arXiv: "Demonstration of Decentralized, Physics-Driven Learning"; PDF v-latest header reads "Laboratory Demonstration of ...")
authors: Dillavou, S., Stern, M., Liu, A. J., Durian, D. J.
venue: Physical Review Applied 18, 014040 (published 2022-07-18); arXiv v1 31 Jul 2021
claim: A 16-edge twin network of variable resistors trains itself by coupled learning, without a processor or external memory, on allostery, regression and iris classification (above 95%; logistic regression gets 98%). In a damage test, edges were cut one at a time every 100 training steps; each cut caused an error spike followed by recovery. The authors deliberately biased resistance drift upward to avoid high-power solutions. When switching between tasks the network quickly erases memory of previous ones. They claim a lab network of only 500 edges would outpace its in-silico counterpart.
check: All claims supported by full text. Iris: "able to classify the iris dataset with over 95% accuracy... logistic regression on this data achieves a test accuracy of 98%". Bias: "We purposefully bias this drift of resistor values to increase on average... avoid high-power solutions". Forgetting: "The network quickly erases memory of previous tasks". Damage: "We track resistance values of five edges, removing one every 100 training steps"; Fig.5: spikes then recovery. Abstract: "a laboratory network of only 500 edges will already outpace its in silico counterpart". 16-edge twin (free/clamped) digipot network, no central processor or external storage.
relevance: Edge removal during learning in a physical learner has been demonstrated, but only as random damage in a tiny network. Importance-guided learning-time pruning (our Paper-1 idea or hub-allocation budgets) in a CLLN seems untested, which leaves room for novelty. The upward resistance bias is a physical subtractive pressure (conductance decay) that matches our finding that weight decay gave node perturbation its stability.

title: Efficient On-Chip Learning for Optical Neural Networks Through Power-Aware Sparse Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Jiaqi Gu, Chenghao Feng, Zheng Zhao, Zhoufeng Ying, Ray T. Chen, David Z. Pan (Gu, J. et al.)
venue: AAAI 2021 (vol. 35, no. 9); arXiv preprint first posted Dec 2020 (v3 5 Sep 2021, cs.ET)
claim: Frames on-chip learning for MZI-mesh optical networks as resource-constrained, noisy zeroth-order optimization, using sparse coordinate descent, mixed training (only a fraction of phase shifters is active) and power-aware dynamic pruning of update steps. The study is emulated in PyTorch with phase-shifter variation (std 2e-3) and thermal crosstalk (2e-3). It optimizes more than 2,500 optical components; with only 5-15% of devices active it recovers accuracy with 3.7-7.6x higher efficiency, and it saves more than 90% of power under device variation and crosstalk.
check: Abstract (also in Crossref record for the DOI): "first to optimize over 2,500 optical components on chip... 3.7x-7.6x higher efficiency, and save >90% power under practical device variations and thermal crosstalk." The experiments section says it is "implemented in PyTorch"; it sets "std. of phase variation ... to 2e-3 and the mutual-coupling factor ... to 2e-3 only for adjacent MZIs". It also says "only a small fraction (5%-15%) of devices is necessary". The method is SZO-SCD (sparse coordinate descent) with mixed active/passive training and power-aware dynamic pruning. All claimed numbers check out.
relevance: Already shows the 'emulator with a device-power scoreboard' approach for a non-von-Neumann substrate, with sparsity and pruning paying off in device power. A photonic-emulator version of our Paper-1 claim would therefore be incremental. Related tool: L2ight (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2110.14807; code at github.com/JeremieMelo/L2ight, newest commit 2021-11-10).

title: Control-free and efficient integrated photonic neural networks via hardware-aware training and pruning
authors: Tengji Xu, Weipeng Zhang, Jiawei Zhang, ... Bhavin J. Shastri, Paul R. Prucnal, Chaoran Huang (Xu, T. et al.)
venue: Optica 11(8), 1039 (2024; published 2024-07-23); arXiv v1 Jan 2024, v2 7 Mar 2024
claim: Hardware-aware training plus pruning pushes the parameters of a microring-based photonic network into its noise-robust, energy-efficient region. In experiment it gains 4 bits of computing precision without device control and raises handwritten-digit accuracy from 67.0% to 95.0% without a thermoelectric controller, with about 10x lower energy. The method is also extended to PCM-based networks.
check: Abstract and full text (pdftotext) confirm everything: "improves the accuracy of experimental handwritten digit classification from 67.0% to 95.0% ... without a thermoelectric controller ... reduces the energy by tenfold." The 4-bit precision gain and the PCM extension are also stated. Small fixes are needed. (1) The 10x is tuning power ("10-fold tuning power consumption reduction"). (2) The PCM result comes from simulation only (MNIST 63.2% -> 98.5%, weight precision 3.99 -> 6.40 bits), not from an experiment. (3) An extra result: on CIFAR-10, accuracy rises from 9.15% to 80.6% with 160x less power, also in simulation.
relevance: Shows pruning paying off through costs specific to the substrate (thermal control, static power) on real photonic hardware, although training is model-based (offline) rather than local. Together with CHAMP (OFC 2022, doi:10.1364/OFC.2022.M2G.3: 99.45% of parameters pruned, static power cut by 98.23%, negligible accuracy loss), it pre-empts any claim that pruning saves energy on photonic hardware. Our novelty would have to be the local or learning-time rule, not the energy saving.

title: Physical learning of power-efficient solutions (arXiv v1); published as "Training self-learning circuits for power-efficient solutions"
authors: Stern, M., Dillavou, S., Jayaraman, D., Durian, D. J., Liu, A. J.
venue: arXiv preprint (submitted 16 Oct 2023); published in APL Machine Learning 2(1), 016114 (27 Feb 2024)
claim: The arXiv title is 'Physical learning of power-efficient solutions'. In resistor-network learners, the power of the trained free state scales linearly with the conductance scale, so a low initial conductance gives lower-power solutions with unchanged training time unless conductances are near the hardware minimum. A modified local coupled-learning rule that minimizes error plus lambda times power produces an error-power trade-off, shown analytically, in simulation and in experiment: more power reduction costs accuracy. At lambda=1 it reduces to the directed-aging rule. Training energy can also be reduced. The tasks are regressions in small networks.
check: Full text checked. Free-state power falls linearly as the conductance scale drops. Training time stays about flat until initialization nears k_min, then grows linearly. Training energy has an optimal initialization. The modified local rule is Eq. 9, and "If we set λ = 1, the free state power cancels out and we recover the directed aging learning rule". Error rises as λ² while power falls linearly in λ, shown in theory, simulation (N=64) and experiment: "greater power reductions can be achieved at the cost of decreasing solution accuracy". Training energy also falls with λ.
relevance: This is the physical counterpart of our weight-decay finding: in resistive learners a power penalty is a local decay term that directly means cost. It supports putting power on the scoreboard and testing pruning or decay as a power knob. It also warns that the result is a trade-off, not a free lunch, so a positive result must be stated as error at fixed power or power at fixed error.

title: Iteratively reweighted least squares and slime mold dynamics: connection and convergence (arXiv v1 title: IRLS and Slime Mold: Equivalence and Convergence)
authors: Damian Straszak, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi
venue: arXiv 2016-01-12; Mathematical Programming 194(1-2):685-717 (online 2021-04-05, print July 2022)
claim: Shows that Physarum (slime-mold) tube dynamics, where tubes thicken with flux and decay otherwise, and IRLS from compressed sensing are projections of the same higher-dimensional dynamical system. Both find the minimum-l1-norm solution in an affine subspace (sparse recovery). This yields a convergence proof and complexity bounds for a damped IRLS. Relatedly, Bonifaci et al. (J. Theor. Biol. 2012, doi:10.1016/j.jtbi.2012.06.017) proved that the Tero et al. model converges to the shortest path whatever the network or initial mass.
check: Abstract: "Both of these dynamics are geared towards finding a minimum l1-norm solution in an affine subspace... the two dynamics are projections of the same dynamical system in higher dimensions." Also proves convergence and complexity bounds for damped IRLS. Matches the claim.
relevance: Supports the premise that local pruning in a flow medium reaches the global optimum, but only for convex (l1/LP-type) objectives. It also offers a theoretical lens: a use-driven subtractive rule acts as an implicit l1 sparse solver, which could frame hub-allocation budgets as reweighted-l1 pruning.

title: Global Optimization, Local Adaptation, and the Role of Growth in Distribution Networks
authors: Henrik Ronellenfitsch and Eleni Katifori
venue: Physical Review Letters 117, 138301 (2016); arXiv physics.bio-ph
claim: Ronellenfitsch & Katifori (PRL 2016; only two authors, so drop 'et al.'). Flow networks with local positive-feedback conductivity adaptation, where vessels thicken with flow and decay otherwise, usually get stuck in disordered, low-efficiency local minima. Coupling the adaptation to uniform growth of the substrate drives the network to hierarchical, low-energy states comparable to simulated annealing, and makes the outcome largely independent of initial conditions (the 'deterministic phase'). The paper says this is equivalent to a slow rise in perfusion or load. The network itself is still pruned from a dense initial plexus; growth does not add or regrow edges. Growth acts as a schedule that gradually suppresses background production, so the strongest-flow edges commit first. The background note stands: optimal networks under steady load are tree-like, and loops appear under damage or fluctuating load (Katifori, Szollosi & Magnasco, PRL 104, 048704, 2010; also Corson, PRL 104, 048703, 2010). The paper also notes that fluctuating sources during adaptation can produce loops. Implication for us: a pruning-only rule may need an annealing-like schedule (a slowly rising load, or slowly falling background/regularization) rather than an additive regrowth phase. This is an untested hypothesis.
check: Metadata confirmed via Crossref (DOI) and arXiv PDF v4. Abstract: "coarse grained models for flow networks with local positive feedback rules for the vessel conductivity typically get trapped in low efficiency, local minima"; growth "can drive the system to a dramatically improved optimal state". Full text: adaptation with growth "can find an energetically comparable minimum to simulated annealing". Katifori et al. PRL 104, 048704 (2010) is ref [10], cited for loops under damage/fluctuating load. Main claim holds. But the 'growth' is not an additive phase that adds edges. It is uniform growth of the tissue substrate, which the paper says is equivalent to a time-dependent rise in perfusion or source strength. The network still starts as a dense plexus and is pruned. Growth exponentially suppresses the background production term, so larger veins lock in first and smaller ones later.
relevance: Counter to 'local subtractive adaptation reaches global optima' in general: subtraction alone gets stuck, and growth (an additive phase) or fluctuation is needed. This suggests our subtractive-only hub-allocation rule may need a growth or regrowth phase. It is one candidate explanation, not a tested one, for why it failed on the BN-CNN.

title: Backpropagation-free training of deep physical neural networks
authors: Momeni, A., Rahmani, B., Malléjac, M., del Hougne, P., Fleury, R.
claim: PhyLL ('model-free forward-forward' in arXiv v1) runs both forward passes on the physical system and needs no model of the nonlinear physical layer. arXiv v1 numbers: an acoustic chaotic-cavity network reaches 94.23% test on vowels (97.62% train), while in-silico training peaks at 60%. A multimode-fiber optical network reaches 97.21% test on MNIST. After perturbing the transmission matrix of a 6-layer optical network, physics-aware BP oscillates around 55% even for small perturbations, while PhyLL recovers within a few epochs. The paper also claims faster training, less digital computation and lower power than hardware-aware training.
check: Metadata confirmed (arXiv v1 PDF header; Crossref for DOI, Science issue 6676, print date 2023-12-15). The Science abstract confirms PhyLL works "without detailed knowledge of the nonlinear physical layer's properties". It also claims gains in training speed, robustness and power. v1 calls the method "model-free forward-forward (MF-FF) training". v1 text: "MF-FF executes both forward passes through the physical hardware, rather than digital models". In the acoustic-PNN figure, the vowel-task labels read 94.23% and 97.62%. In the optics-PNN figure, the MNIST panel reads 97.21%. For the 6-layer optics-PNN with a Gaussian-perturbed transmission matrix, v1 says "PA-BP struggles to restore accuracy". It adds that MF-FF "can easily recover accuracy after a few epochs". The in-silico peak (60%) and the PA-BP oscillation level (55%) are inline numbers, and pdftotext dropped their digits ("only a maximum ... of %", "oscillates around %"). The qualitative statements are confirmed, but those two values could not be read.
relevance: The strongest published case of a BP-free rule beating model-based BP on robustness. But the win is against BP with a wrong or outdated model, not against ideal BP. To reproduce it in an emulator we must inject a reality gap (model mismatch, drift, perturbations); our GPU benchmark had none. The numbers are from arXiv v1 and the Science version may differ.

title: Multiplexed gradient descent: Fast online training of modern datasets on hardware neural networks without backpropagation
authors: McCaughan, A. N.; Oripov, B. G.; Ganesh, N.; Nam, S. W.; Dienstfrey, A.; Buckley, S. M. (NIST)
venue: arXiv v1 5 Mar 2023; published APL Machine Learning 1, 026118 (June 2023)
claim: A model-free, zeroth-order perturbative framework (SPSA or finite differences) for training analog or digital hardware, evaluated in simulation. Same small networks with MSE and SGD without momentum: CIFAR-10 3-layer CNN reaches 60.7% after 1e7 steps vs BP 68%; Fashion-MNIST 86.1% vs 88.6%. It tolerates noise and device-to-device activation variation; with variation a=0.25, NIST7x7 took about 2x longer to train. Table 3 converts steps into time. To reach the same CIFAR-10 accuracy: HW1 (thermo-optic photonics, perturbation time 1 ms) 5.6 h vs CPU/GPU BP 480 s; HW2 (mem-compute or analog VLSI, 10 ns) 200 ms; HW3 (superconducting or athermal photonics, 200 ps) 4 ms.
check: I read the full text of arXiv v1 with pdftotext -raw, and Crossref confirms the DOI, venue, volume and article number. Table 2: CIFAR-10 3-layer CNN reaches 60.7% at 1e7 steps vs backprop 68%. The Fashion-MNIST 2-layer CNN gets 83.4-86.1% at 1e7 steps depending on tau_theta; 86.1% is the best setting (tau_theta=1000), vs backprop 88.6%. Section 3.6: "we used a basic stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer without momentum. Both strategies used a mean squared error (MSE) cost function." On activation variation: "functions (a = 0.25), the network only took about twice as much time to fully train the NIST7x7 dataset"; a>0.25 failed to converge. Table 3 (read in raw mode, because the layout mode scrambles the rows): perturbation time tau_p is 1 ms / 10 ns / 200 ps for HW1/HW2/HW3. Parameter-update time is 1 ms / 1 us / 200 ps, and input-sample update time is 100 ns / 1 ns / 10 ps. CIFAR-10 training time (1e7 steps) is 5.6 h / 200 ms / 4 ms, vs backprop 480 s. The caption says the final column is the time backprop on a standard GPU or CPU takes to reach the same accuracy. The hardware examples match the claim. The paper describes finite-difference, coordinate descent, SPSA and analog variants as instances of the MGD framework, and all results are simulations.
relevance: Direct precedent for rescoring a weight-perturbation-type learner on machine time constants. It confirms our finding that perturbative learners lose accuracy (our node perturbation got 11-14% A_AUC) and shows they win on time only when perturbation and update times are well below 1 us; on thermo-optic hardware they lose. It pre-empts a time-only rescoring, so a new contribution would need modeled energy, a memory-bound or continual setting, or the subtractive element.

title: Deep physical neural networks trained with backpropagation
authors: Wright, L. G., Onodera, T., Stein, M. M., Wang, T., Schachter, D. T., Hu, Z., McMahon, P. L.
venue: arXiv preprint 2021-04-27 (cs.LG); published Nature 601, 549-555 (2022)
claim: Physics-aware training (PAT) is a hybrid: the forward pass runs on the physical system and the backward pass uses a differentiable digital model. On a second-harmonic-generation optical network, in-silico training gives vowel accuracy barely above random, while PAT reaches 93%; as more physical layers are added, in-silico training fails while PAT keeps working. MNIST reaches 87% (mechanical), 93% (electronic) and 97% (optical SHG; the physical transforms raise a roughly 90% digital-only baseline to 97%). Code: github.com/mcmahon-lab/Physics-Aware-Training (newest commit 2024-09-30).
check: Read the full text of arXiv v1 via pdftotext. Crossref confirms the Nature title, volume 601, pages 549-555, published 2022-01-26, first author Logan G. Wright. Fig. 3 caption: "in silico training results in accuracy barely distinguishable from random guessing, while PAT permits training the physical device to realize 93% accuracy. As physical layers are added, in silico training fails". The main text puts in-silico's best vowel accuracy at ~40% (7 classes). The Fig. 4 caption gives "Final test accuracy is 87%, 93% and 97% for mechanical, electrical, and optics-based PNNs". SHG "boosts the performance of the digital operations from roughly 90% accuracy to 97%". In PAT the physical system runs the forward pass, and a differentiable digital model estimates the gradients in the backward pass. The paper also says PAT makes the trained models resilient to noise. The GitHub commits.atom feed for mcmahon-lab/Physics-Aware-Training shows the newest commit on 2024-09-30.
relevance: Counter to the premise that non-von-Neumann substrates require BP-free rules: BP with an approximate digital twin works on real hardware and mitigates noise. In any emulator comparison, the baseline must include PAT-style hybrid BP (with its digital-model cost and data movement), not just ideal BP or in-silico BP.

title: Physical deep learning with biologically inspired training method: gradient-free approach for physical hardware (arXiv v1 title: "Physical Deep Learning with Biologically Plausible Training Method")
authors: Nakajima, M., Inoue, K., Tanaka, K., Kuniyoshi, Y., Hashimoto, T., Nakajima, K.
venue: Nature Communications 13, 7847 (published 2022-12-26); arXiv preprint April 2022
claim: Augmented DFA (random projection with an arbitrary nonlinearity g(x), no knowledge of the system's gradient) trains an FPGA-assisted optoelectronic deep reservoir computer. BP with a mismatched derivative diverges or fails to learn (negative correlation gives no learning), while augmented DFA always converges (about 89% even in its worst case). Experiment: MNIST 97.80%, Fashion-MNIST 85.91%, CIFAR-10 47.83% (simulation: 99.03 / 86.31 / 56.85, arXiv version). Measured end-to-end training time per image beats a Xeon CPU beyond about 5,000 nodes (vs CPU BP) and about 10,000 nodes (vs CPU augmented DFA). On the benchtop, FPGA data transfer and DAC/ADC take about 92% of the time, while the optoelectronic computation takes about 0.02%.
check: All numbers verified in the arXiv full text: sim 99.03/86.31/56.85, exp 97.80/85.91/47.83 (MNIST/F-MNIST/CIFAR-10). Timing: "FPGA processing (data-transfer, memory allocation, and DAC/ADC) of ~92%... optoelectronic processing time of ~0.02%"; acceleration beyond CPU (Xeon W-2145) "at N ~5,000 and ~10,000 for the BP and augmented DFA algorithm, respectively".
relevance: Supports DFA-type learners (we already have DFA) on physical substrates when the device derivative is unknown. It also shows the real bottleneck is I/O at the von Neumann interface, which an emulator scoreboard must model explicitly. CIFAR-10 accuracy remains far below BP CNNs.

title: Integrated photonic neural network with on-chip backpropagation training

title: The backpropagation algorithm implemented on spiking neuromorphic hardware

venue: arXiv preprint 2021 (v1 13 Jun 2021); published Nature Communications 15, 9691 (8 Nov 2024)

check: Numbers match the published Nature Comms version, not arXiv v2. The published text says: "average inference accuracy of 95.7% after 60 epochs (best of 3 runs in any epoch: 96.3%)", "1.5 ms (0.17 ms for inference only)", "0.6 mJ", "EDP of 0.88 μJs", "0.0025 mJ", "on-chip learning engine is responsible for most power consumption", "two orders of magnitude power savings in the case of small batch sizes", and "novel approaches should at least surpass the given performance and power metrics". Fashion-MNIST gives 79%, against 84.4% for an ANN of the same size.

Backprop is also moving onto neuromorphic chips elsewhere: EventProp on SpiNNaker2 (arXiv:2412.15021) and on BrainScaleS-2 (arXiv:2302.07141), and a 2026 neuromorphic training chip with dedicated BP engines (doi:10.1038/s41467-026-70586-x). title: In-Hardware Learning of Multilayer Spiking Neural Networks on a Neuromorphic Processor

Table I (Loihi vs Python) FA: MNIST 94.5/98.9, F-MNIST 84.3/92.7, CIFAR-10 61.6/64.2. DFA: 94.7/98.9, 84.8/92.5, 62.2/64.4. DFA came out slightly better than FA on chip (fewer quantized stages), and 8-bit weights cost 2-8 points. The energy edge over the GPU was shown only at batch 1. title: E-prop on SpiNNaker 2: Exploring online learning in spiking RNNs on neuromorphic hardware

venue: Frontiers in Neuroscience 16:1018006 (published 2022-11-28; PMC9742366)

In the paper's memory analysis, e-prop with 360 neurons needs 4.3 MB and BPTT with 256 neurons needs 2.7 MB for roughly equal accuracy at the default sequence length. Abstract: "accuracy of 91.12% while requiring only 680 KB of memory for training the network with 25 K weights", and "12 times less energy than using a NVIDIA V100 GPU". The network is 120 recurrent neurons on 12 PEs (ARM cores). Training 30 epochs in real time takes 586 h 27 min ("more than 24 days"). Memory: "E-prop with 360 neurons needs 4.3 MB and BPTT with 256 neurons needs 2.7 MB memory". Crossover: "after 600 time steps E-prop uses less memory". relevance: This runs parallel to our equal-memory GPU result, on a neuromorphic machine. A local online rule beats backprop on memory only for long temporal streams; on short or static inputs, BPTT wins at equal memory. That points to the regime where an honest local-rule win is plausible: long sequences under per-core memory caps. The energy win is an estimate that comes with a large wall-clock cost. A related ASIC is ReckOn (arXiv:2208.09759): e-prop-like on-chip learning in 0.45 mm2 with under 150 uW training power and 0.8% memory overhead.

title: Demonstrating Advantages of Neuromorphic Computation: A Pilot Study
authors: Timo Wunderlich et al.
venue: arXiv Nov 2018 (v4 Mar 2019); published Frontiers in Neuroscience 13:260, 2019

That is the honest framing for an emulator study. In-the-loop BrainScaleS-2 training (Cramer et al., PNAS 2022, doi:10.1073/pnas.2109194119) reaches 97.6% on 16x16 MNIST at 2.4 uJ per inference and under 200 mW, but gradients are computed on the host (von Neumann). A recent Loihi 2 counterpart is fully on-chip Q-learning (arXiv:2609.32317): half the CPU's execution time with 2 orders of magnitude less dynamic power.

title: Emulating Brain-like Rapid Learning in Neuromorphic Edge Computing
authors: Kenneth Stewart, Michael Neumeier, Sumit Bam Shrestha, Garrick Orchard, Emre Neftci

Lava-DL "includes a functional differentiable simulator of the Intel Loihi's neuron dynamics, and quantization-aware training with the same stochastic rounding and precision used in the Loihi chip." SOEL hyperparameters were meta-trained with MAML. The last layer was learned on Loihi 1 with accuracy "comparable to the Lava-DL SOEL models", and the same was done in Lava's software simulation of Loihi 2 plasticity. On PyPI, lava-nc 0.10.0 and lava-dl 0.6.0 require Python >=3.10,<3.11, which matches the project venv; they were not installed. The simulators give functional fidelity, not energy, so energy still needs a separate published model. It also shows on-chip local learning is mostly readout adaptation on top of an offline-trained body.

title: Brian2Loihi: An emulator for the neuromorphic chip Loihi using the spiking neural network simulator Brian
authors: Carlo Michaelis, Andrew B. Lehr, Winfried Oed, Christian Tetzlaff

On-chip learning is also reviewed and implemented, with reasonable discrepancy due to stochastic rounding." It also describes an "open source Loihi emulator based on the neural network simulator Brian". The claim matches.

It could run our local rules under Loihi's integer and trace constraints on the local PC, with energy taken from a published per-operation model rather than measured. Limits: Loihi 1 only, and unmaintained (PyPI brian2-loihi 0.5.2 dated 2021-07; last GitHub commit 2021-12-06).

title: Memory-Efficient Deep Learning on a SpiNNaker 2 Prototype

venue: Frontiers in Neuroscience 12:840 (published 2018-11-16)

Active connectivity stays fixed at 1.3% throughout training (1%, 3% and 30% per layer: smaller matrices are denser). The network reaches 96.6% on MNIST using under 4% of a fully connected network's memory. Power and energy are about 2 orders of magnitude lower than an x86 CPU (2% of its power). check: Full text (Europe PMC PMC6250847) supports the core claims: "trained entirely within this constraint without the use of external memory. Throughout training, the proportion of active connections is limited to 1.3%." Per-layer connectivity fixed at 1, 3, 30% (smaller matrix, denser). MNIST 96.6% vs 98.2% fully connected (FC not trainable on chip); "<4% memory compared to a fully connected network, and only 2% of the power budget" vs X86. Power reduced 2 orders of magnitude (87.9 mW single core); energy was 3.7% (1P), 2.2% (1PA), 1.2% (4PA) of X86, i.e. roughly 1.5 to 2 orders. CIFAR-10 only estimated: "about 10 cores (640 KB of SRAM) are required", not run. Footprint 36.63 KB of 64 KB data SRAM (the 64 KB is the data half of a 128 KB per-PE SRAM).

The budget was allocated per layer, not per neuron by activity, so hub allocation is still open on hardware. There was no equal-memory comparison with dense or checkpointed BP and no GPU baseline, which leaves room for an honest scoreboard study.

title: Structural plasticity on an accelerated analog neuromorphic hardware system
authors: Sebastian Billaudelle, Benjamin Cramer, Mihai A. Petrovici, Korbinian Schreiber, David Kappel, Johannes Schemmel, Karlheinz Meier
venue: Neural Networks 133:11-20 (published Jan 2021); arXiv preprint first posted Dec 2019 (v2 Sep 2020)
claim: Fully local structural plasticity (prune below threshold, re-seed new partners) runs on the BrainScaleS-2 on-chip processor. It keeps each neuron's fan-in constant and the connectome sparse. On a small supervised task (Iris), accuracy reaches up to 92.3% and stays at about 92% across sparsity levels. Six realized synapses match accuracy otherwise needing more than 32. One epoch takes 137 ms (under 50 ms without host overhead), about a 500x speed-up. Fan-in is a fixed per-neuron resource on many chips: 256 on TrueNorth/ODIN, 64/256 on DYNAP-SEL, 32 on the prototype and 256 on the full BrainScaleS-2.
check: Full text (arXiv v2) checked. Abstract: "constantly rewiring the pre- and postsynaptic partners while keeping the neuronal fan-in constant and the connectome sparse", run on the on-chip embedded processor. The text gives "up to 92.3 % for structural plasticity with a bundle size of 8" and "approximately 92 % for all of the sparsity levels". It also says "only six synapses were sufficient to reach levels of accuracy otherwise only tangible with more than 32 synapses". On speed: "137 ms ... less than 50 ms, which corresponds to a speedup factor of about 500". Fan-in figures: TrueNorth and ODIN 256; DYNAP-SEL 64 static synapses on four cores and 256 learning synapses on a fifth; prototype 32; full BrainScaleS-2 256, with optional neuron merging. Pruning is threshold-based and the task is Iris (petal features).
relevance: This is the closest hardware precedent for per-neuron connection budgets, but with the opposite policy to hub allocation: a uniform, fixed fan-in. On analog chips, synapses physically belong to neurons, so activity-proportional budgets are hard to realize except by merging neuron circuits. Hub allocation fits better on digital chips where synapse memory is pooled per core. Only a toy-scale task was shown.

title: Connection Pruning for Deep Spiking Neural Networks with On-Chip Learning
authors: Thao N.N. Nguyen, Bharadwaj Veeravalli, Xuanyao Fong
venue: ICONS 2021 (International Conference on Neuromorphic Systems), ACM, July 27-29 2021; arXiv v1 Oct 2020, v3 31 Jul 2021

Inference: 2.83x and 78.24%. FPGA (Zynq-7000) power overhead 0.56%. Method is pruning during on-chip STDP learning (dynamic pruning plus post-learning pruning per layer) on a 3-conv-layer TTFS SNN.

This overlaps with 'prune while learning on chip', but uses STDP rather than BP/DFA and makes no equal-budget comparison with backprop.

title: Online Continual Learning on Intel Loihi 2 via a Co-designed Spiking Neural Network
authors: Elvin Hajizada, Danielle Rager, Timothy Shea, Leobardo Campos-Macias, Andreas Wild, Eyke Hüllermeier, Yulia Sandamirskaya, Mike Davies

title: Limitations in odour recognition and generalization in a neuromorphic olfactory circuit

venue: arXiv preprint (v1 20 Sep 2023, cs.NE); published as Matters Arising in Nature Machine Intelligence 6(12):1451-1453, 16 Dec 2024
claim: A Matters Arising critique of Imam & Cleland's (2020) Loihi olfactory-bulb (EPL) 'rapid online learning' model. The authors re-ran the released code in software simulation.
