The dataset was recorded in gas-specific batches over nine months, and sensor drift makes classification possible even before the gas is released. With baseline subtraction, the model fails to generalise across repeated presentations of the same gas, even without noise. An 8-line Python hash table (dictionary) matches or exceeds EPL in recognition accuracy and beats it in runtime. The original authors replied (Moyal, Imam & Cleland, doi:10.1038/s42256-024-00951-2).
check: Abstract and full text (pdftotext) read. Abstract supports drift/non-randomised protocol, poor generalisation over repeated presentations, and "can be solved with a simple hash table approach, matching or exceeding the reported results in accuracy and runtime." One wording error: the replication was NOT run on Loihi. They "repeated the simulations" using "the code released by the authors" on CPU; the Loihi runtime in their comparison figure is quoted from the original paper. The hash-table comparison is against EPL on CPU and the reported Loihi time. Other details: with baseline subtraction, "recognition across repetitions failed even for samples without any noise occlusion". Drift alone allows "successful gas classification before the gas is presented". The reply by Moyal, Imam & Cleland (doi:10.1038/s42256-024-00951-2, NMI 6:1454-1456) was confirmed via Crossref.
relevance: A cautionary precedent for on-chip learning claims. Any learning advantage we report on an emulator needs trivial baselines (hash, kNN, NCM) and leak- and drift-controlled data, or it can be overturned.

title: Are SNNs Really More Energy-Efficient Than ANNs? an In-Depth Hardware-Aware Study
authors: Manon Dampfhoffer, Thomas Mesquida, Alexandre Valentian, Lorena Anghel
venue: IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence 7(3):731-741 (June 2023)
claim: Many SNN energy claims ignore memory accesses or compare against naive ANN hardware. With a theoretical upper bound on ANN data reuse and sparsity, plus the Eyeriss accelerator as a case study, IF-neuron SNNs compete only at very high spike sparsity: 0.15-1.38 spikes per synapse per inference, depending on the ANN implementation. LIF and continuous-synapse models are worse than IF.
check: The abstract supports every part of the claim. It says many studies "do not consider memory accesses ... use naive ANN hardware implementations". The paper gives a theoretical upper bound from ANN data reuse and sparsity and uses Eyeriss as a case study. IF SNNs compete "when there is a very high spike sparsity, i.e. between 0.15 and 1.38 spikes per synapse per inference, depending on the ANN implementation." It also says "the simpler IF model is more energy-efficient than the Leaky IF and temporal continuous synapse models."
relevance: If our emulator scoreboard counts SOPs against MACs, it has to include memory traffic and data reuse, or it will overstate the neuromorphic side. It also gives a sparsity threshold to check. Davidson & Furber 2021 (doi:10.3389/fnins.2021.651141) reach the same verdict: most rate-coded SNNs are not more efficient than the source ANN on the same silicon.

title: Benchmarking Neuromorphic Hardware and Its Energy Expenditure
authors: Christoph Ostrau, Christian Klarhorst, Michael Thies, Ulrich Rückert
venue: Frontiers in Neuroscience 16:873935 (PMC9201569)
claim: SNABSuite is a cross-platform benchmark covering NEST, GeNN on CPU/GPU, SpiNNaker, Spikey and BrainScaleS, including an STDP-based learning benchmark. Its energy model, built from per-component measured costs (idle, per neuron, per spike, per synaptic event, STDP activation), predicts a network's energy on a target system 'without actually having access to it'. In the scaled brain-simulation comparison the analog system was most efficient, while SpiNNaker was on par with CPUs and less efficient than the GPU. Current neuromorphic systems are at least 4 orders of magnitude less efficient than the brain.
check: Abstract: model "enables the prediction of the energy expenditure of a network on a target system without actually having access to it"; neuromorphic "at least four orders of magnitude less efficient". Full text: "The results demonstrate the superiority of the analogue system... SpiNNaker performs on par with both CPUs and is less efficient compared to the GPU." Energy model components are idle power, per idle neuron, per spike, per spike transmission, and static STDP power plus energy per synaptic event. The STDP SLAM benchmark is real: "All tested platforms demonstrate the successful learning of the surroundings using the STDP".
relevance: A direct precedent for the project rule that energy is only a model-based estimate. It also counters any assumption that digital neuromorphic beats a GPU by default.

title: Open the box of digital neuromorphic processor: Towards effective algorithm-hardware co-design
authors: Guangzhi Tang, Ali Safa, Kevin Shidqi, ..., Amirreza Yousefzadeh (imec / KU Leuven)
venue: 2023 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS); arXiv v1 27 Mar 2023
claim: Publishes instruction-level and component-level energy for the SENeCA digital neuromorphic processor (GF-22nm FDX, pre-silicon RTL power within 15% of signoff). Per micro-kernel: IF neuron 12.7/13.2 pJ, Hebbian learning 15.5 pJ, e-prop gradient learning 22.9/19.2 pJ. A synaptic op costs 12.7 pJ (BF16, one event) or 7.0 pJ (four events), against 23 pJ cited for Loihi. It shows how to estimate task energy by counting instructions, including an online Hebbian learning example.
check: Full text checked. Table III: IF 12.7/13.2, Hebbian 15.5/15.5, gradient (e-prop) 22.9/19.2 pJ. Table IV: BF16 synop 12.7 pJ (1 event), 7.0 pJ (4 events), Loihi 23 pJ. Measured with Cadence JOULES "RTL level power measurement tool (within 15% of signoff power)", GF-22nm FDX. Sec. IV-B estimates energy "by counting the number of instructions executed" for online Hebbian digit classification. Crossref confirms the DOI, title and ISCAS 2023.
relevance: The most explicit public cost table found for learning rules on a digital neuromorphic processor. It would let an instruction-count energy model of our local learners (Hebbian or e-prop-like vs dense BP) run on the local PC, in line with the model-based-estimate rule. A complementary runtime model: a max-affine roofline model of Loihi 2 compute and communication with Pearson >= 0.97 against measured runtime (Timcheck et al. 2026, arXiv:2601.10035).

title: Biologically Plausible Learning on Neuromorphic Hardware Architectures
authors: Christopher Wolters, Brady Taylor, Edward Hanson, Xiaoxuan Yang, Ulf Schlichtmann, Yiran Chen
venue: arXiv Dec 2022 (v2 11 Apr 2023); published in 2023 IEEE 66th MWSCAS, pp. 733-737
claim: Uses DNN+NeuroSim (RRAM compute-in-memory, in-situ training, MNIST MLPs) to compare BP and DFA head-to-head; the authors call it the first such comparison on CIM hardware. Accuracy: BP is best, especially under hardware imperfections. With cycle-to-cycle conductance variation swept from 1% to 5%, BP still converged; DFA worked only at 1%. DFA needs an ADC of at least 3 bits, and narrow layers hurt it (final accuracy at width 8: DFA 0.08 vs BP 0.44; at width 256: 0.79 vs 0.80). Energy: about 95% goes to off-chip buffer accesses for activations, errors and gradients. These accesses are the same for BP and DFA, so energy is virtually identical. Latency: 91% comes from buffering, and weight-gradient computation plus writing is 96%. Because DFA updates layers in parallel, the BP/DFA latency ratio approaches N for N layers. Area: the CIM arrays take under 1% of the chip. ADCs dominate BP's area (about 52.7%) because reads must be transposable; weight-gradient units dominate DFA's area (about 53.1%).
check: I read the full text (arXiv v2) and checked the DOI on Crossref. Every number matches. C2C variation: "Sweeping typical ranges from 1% to 5%... BP converges to comparable accuracies... whereas DFA performs well only for 1% deviation." ADC: "At least a 3-bit ADC is required." Table I: width 8 gives DFA 0.08 / BP 0.44; width 256 gives 0.79 / 0.80. Energy: "95% share is allocated to accessing off-chip buffers... resulting in virtually the same energy consumption." Latency: buffering is 91%; weight-gradient computation plus writing is 96%; the BP/DFA ratio "approaches a scaling factor of N." Area: CIM is under 1%; ADC is 52.7% for BP and WGU is 53.1% for DFA. The paper's own "first" claim reads "first to compare the impact of different learning algorithms on Compute-In-Memory-based hardware".
relevance: This is the closest existing BP-vs-BP-free comparison on a calibrated AIMC cost model. The BP-free rule wins only on latency, not on accuracy or energy, because activations and errors are still buffered off-chip. If we port our NP/FG/DFA learners, the scoreboard will reproduce this result unless (i) the emulator applies the update in the array immediately, without buffering activations (an online batch-1 setting), or (ii) we count ADC conversions and transposed reads. DFA's sensitivity to update noise predicts the same or worse for NP/FG.

title: Forward-only learning in memristor arrays with month-scale stability
authors: Adrien Renaudineau, Mamadou Hawa Diallo, Theo Dupuis, Bastien Imbert, ... Damien Querlioz (15 authors)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.ET); v1 Jan 2026, v3 dated 5 Sep 2026
claim: Experiments on filamentary HfOx/Ti memristor arrays of up to 8,064 devices, using a hardware-in-the-loop protocol: all reads and writes are physical, while multilayer MACs are emulated from measured conductances. Task: a 4-class ImageNet-resolution transfer task. Supervised Forward-Forward reached 89.5% (sd 1.4) and single-pass competitive forward 89.6% (sd 1.8), versus a BP reference on the same devices at 90.0% (sd 1.1); the differences are not significant. Mean pulse count per device was similar for FF and BP; only the layer-wise distribution was inverted. Updates are sign-only, threshold-triggered single sub-1 V RESET pulses: 0.84 pJ per pulse on optimized devices vs 387 pJ for program-and-verify (460x less), and only 46% more energy than inference-only operation. Reset-trained models stayed stable for one month and through 25 h of read-disturb, whereas the Write&Verify baseline lost about 3 points.
check: The full text (v3 PDF) supports every number. Abstract: "hardware-in-the-loop protocol on arrays up to 8,064 devices: all conductance reads and programming updates are physical, and multilayer MACs are emulated in software". SFF scores 89.5% (sd 1.4), CF 89.6% (sd 1.8) and BP 90.0% (sd 1.1), each over 5 runs, and the differences are "not statistically significant". "the mean pulse count per device is similar across supervised Forward-Forward and backpropagation", and the layer-wise distribution is inverted. Energy is 0.84 pJ per pulse vs 387 pJ for program-and-verify (460x), "46% more energy than inference-only". Under 25 h read-disturb, the Write&Verify baseline "lost nearly 3 percentage points". Updates are thresholded and sign-only, with a single sub-1 V reset pulse (0.62 V, 30 ns on optimized devices).
relevance: Real-hardware evidence that a BP-free rule can tie BP in accuracy on crossbars, but not that it reduces writes. The energy win comes from the programming primitive, which BP used as well. The forward-only advantage is architectural: no backward pass and no transposed reads. A claim that BP-free learning matches BP on memristors is therefore no longer novel. Our honest win metrics on an emulator would be transposed-read/ADC count or activation memory, not pulse count. Their sign-only threshold update is a ready-made device model to emulate.

title: When Pipelined In-Memory Accelerators Meet Spiking Direct Feedback Alignment: A Co-Design for Neuromorphic Edge Computing
authors: Haoxiong Ren, Yangu He, Kwunhang Wong, Rui Bao, Ning Lin, Zhongrui Wang, Dashan Shang (7 authors)
venue: IEEE/ACM ICCAD 2025 (Crossref: IEEE proceedings, published 2025-10-26, pp. 1-9); arXiv v1 21 Jul 2025, cs.AR
claim: Maps a hardware-friendly spiking DFA (SDFA) onto an RRAM in-memory computing architecture with a three-level pipelined dataflow (PipeSDFA). Accuracy loss is under 2% on five datasets versus baselines. Compared with PipeLayer, a ReRAM BP training accelerator, training time is 1.1x to 10.5x shorter and energy 1.37x to 2.1x lower.
check: Abstract (full text read): "PipeSDFA training accelerator incurs less than 2% accuracy loss on five datasets compared to baselines, while achieving 1.1-10.5x and 1.37-2.1x reductions in training time and energy consumption, respectively compared to PipeLayer". Three-level (Timestep-Data-Batch) pipeline on RRAM IMC confirmed. All numbers match.
relevance: This is the only result found where a BP-free rule beats an analog/ReRAM BP accelerator on both training time and energy, because DFA removes the sequential backward pass and lets layers pipeline. It supports the user's hypothesis but takes away novelty from a 'DFA wins on an IMC simulator' paper. The gains are modest (at most 2.1x energy) and come with an accuracy cost. The work is SNN-specific and compares against PipeLayer, not against Tiki-Taka-style in-array updates.

title: Scaling of hardware-compatible perturbative training algorithms
authors: B. G. Oripov, A. Dienstfrey, A. N. McCaughan, S. M. Buckley (NIST)
venue: arXiv preprint (v1, 26 Jan 2025); published in APL Machine Learning 3, 026107 (Apr 2025)
claim: Extends multiplexed gradient descent (MGD; McCaughan et al., APL Machine Learning 2023, arXiv:2303.03986) to both weight perturbation and node perturbation. On Fashion-MNIST, WP and NP reach the same final accuracy as BP on the same architecture (91.6%). Gradient-estimation time grows with the number of parameters N, but time to reach 80% changed by less than one order of magnitude while network size changed by more than three. NP was about 2x faster than WP to reach 80%, and about 10x faster to reach 50%. The authors estimate 1e9 MGD iterations would take about 16 minutes on 1 MHz hardware. The simulations are hardware-agnostic (no calibrated crossbar model). The 2023 paper reported MGD staying slightly below BP after 1e7 steps and being robust to device-to-device variation.
check: The full text supports the claims. Fig. 4a: "MGD algorithm can match the same final accuracy of 91.6% as backpropagation" on Fashion-MNIST. The paper also says "time to reach 80% accuracy varies by less than one order of magnitude over > 3 orders of magnitude change in network size". It adds "node perturbation is 10x faster to get to 50%", "only 2x faster than weight perturbation to get to 80%" (1M params), and "10^9 MGD time iterations would take 16 minutes on hardware with a modest speed of 1 MHz". The simulations are model-free and generic, with no device or crossbar model. The gradient-estimation time scales with N for WP and with sqrt(N) for NP.
relevance: The strongest evidence that NP/WP can reach BP accuracy when hardware makes each perturb-and-evaluate cycle cheap (ns to us), i.e. when the scoreboard is wall-clock on fast analog hardware rather than GPU FLOPs. However, it uses Fashion-MNIST, not class-incremental CIFAR-10, where our NP reached only 11-14%. It also compares against GPU BP, not analog BP (Tiki-Taka), which also runs at O(1) per sample on crossbars. The idea goes back to Jabri & Flower 1992 (IEEE TNN, DOI:10.1109/72.105429): weight perturbation is cheaper than BP for parallel analog VLSI.

title: Activity-difference training of deep neural networks using memristor crossbars
authors: Su-in Yi, Jack D. Kendall, R. Stanley Williams, Suhas Kumar
venue: Nature Electronics 6, 45-51 (online 21 Nov 2022; issue Jan 2023)
claim: MADEM (memristor activity-difference energy minimization) runs on co-designed tantalum-oxide analog memristor crossbars. It computes local gradients numerically from behavioural differences in the target hardware, via Hopfield-like energy minimization (EP-like). It trained one-layer and multilayer networks to classify Braille words with high accuracy. Modelling projects an energy advantage of more than four orders of magnitude over digital approaches for scaled-up problem sizes (verbatim abstract checked on nature.com).
check: The nature.com abstract matches the claimed content: "numerically calculates local gradients via Hopfield-like energy minimization using behavioural differences in the hardware" and "over four orders of magnitude energy advantage compared with digital approaches for scaled-up problem sizes". It also confirms tantalum oxide crossbars and Braille-word classification with one-layer and multilayer networks. The summary adds that the hardware is 64x64 memristor arrays with integrated CMOS control circuitry.
relevance: Shows that EP/activity-difference training on real crossbars exists. Related work: Kendall et al. 2020 (arXiv:2006.01981) ran EP on SPICE resistive networks, and Doell et al. 2026 (DOI:10.1080/17445760.2026.2616770) found memristor EP needs a resistance range of at least one decade. The 4-orders-of-magnitude figure is against digital hardware, not analog BP, and the tasks are tiny. No head-to-head of EP-family vs Tiki-Taka under the same device model was found; that would be a novel experiment, though EP is not in our current codebase.

title: Fast and robust analog in-memory deep neural network training
authors: Malte J. Rasch, Fabio Carta, Omobayode Fagbohungbe, Tayfun Gokmen (IBM Research)
venue: Nature Communications (published 2024-08-20); preprint arXiv 2023-03-08
claim: Proposes two in-memory training algorithms, Chopped-TTv2 (c-TTv2) and AGAD. Both keep the fast runtime complexity of Tiki-Taka v2: in-array forward pass, transposed backward pass and pulse-coincidence outer-product update. They remove the need for near-perfect reference (zero-point) conductance programming. The paper maps limits in conductance noise, symmetry, retention and endurance. It notes that earlier analog training algorithms either needed substantial auxiliary digital compute (accumulating gradients in floating point) or a precise zero point. The AIHWKit CHANGELOG lists ChoppedTTv2 and AGAD presets.
check: Published abstract (Europe PMC): earlier algorithms "either invoke significant amount of auxiliary digital compute-accumulating the gradient in digital floating point precision ... or suffer from the need for near perfectly programming reference conductance values"; new algorithms "retain the same fast runtime complexity while resolving the requirement of a precise zero point"; limits investigated "in terms of conductance noise, symmetry, retention, and endurance". arXiv v1 full text names c-TTv2 and AGAD, built on TTv2, with pulse-coincidence outer-product update and transposed backward pass. AIHWKit CHANGELOG lists "ChoppedTTv2*, AGAD*" presets (#512). All claims supported.
relevance: This is the analog-BP baseline that any BP-free learner must beat on an AIMC emulator, and it ships with AIHWKit. Wu et al. (NeurIPS 2024, DOI:10.52202/079017-1176, arXiv:2406.12774) prove that plain analog SGD on asymmetric devices has a non-vanishing asymptotic error, while Tiki-Taka converges exactly. Comparing against plain analog SGD would therefore be a strawman. Our comparison must use TT, c-TTv2, AGAD or mixed precision.

title: Pruning random resistive memory for optimizing analog AI (arXiv v1 title: '...optimizing analogue AI')
authors: Yi Li, Songqi Wang, Yaping Zhao, ... Zhongrui Wang, Xiaoxin Xu, Dashan Shang, ... (20 authors on arXiv v1; 23 on the Nature Communications version per Crossref)
venue: arXiv cs.ET, 13 Nov 2023; published in Nature Communications 17:1190 (10 Jan 2026)
claim: Trains randomly weighted RRAM networks by edge-pruning topology optimization instead of weight programming. The random weights come from electroforming stochasticity on a 40 nm, 256K resistive memory macro. Edge scores are updated on a digital processor with backprop (straight-through estimator), and pruned cells are set to near-zero conductance. FashionMNIST CNN: hardware topology optimization reached 87.4%, versus 79.7% for hardware weight optimization with free updates. Under a matched write budget, weight optimization was 17.3 points worse. Topology optimization needed 99.94% fewer weight updates, and 50% sparsity cut RRAM inference energy by 30.6%. Published abstract: +17.3% and +19.9% accuracy (Fashion-MNIST, Spoken Digit), +9.8% PR-AUC (DRIVE), energy reductions of 78.3%, 67.9% and 99.7%, and scaling to ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100.
check: Checked the Nature HTML (abstract, Fig. 3 caption, results text, Methods) and the full arXiv v1 PDF. Everything in the claim holds: 40nm 256K macro, random weights from electroforming stochasticity, pruning by resetting cells to near-zero conductance. Methods: "a general-purpose digital processor computes the gradients... The scores are updated using a straight-through gradient estimator". Results: "hardware TO achieves a classification accuracy of 87.4% compared with 79.7% of hardware WO with free updates". Under a matched write budget (~2.3M updates), WO drops 17.3 points. Weight updates fall 99.94%. RM energy falls 30.6% (12.94 vs 18.65 nJ) because of 0.5 sparsity. The published abstract numbers also match: +17.3%/+19.9%, +9.8% PR-AUC, 78.3/67.9/99.7% energy cut, ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100.
relevance: This already shows, on real RRAM, that subtractive learning pays off on an analog substrate, with device writes as the decisive metric. It strongly supports the user's principle but kills a generic 'prune instead of program to save writes' emulator paper. Remaining openings: their scores are still computed by BP on a digital processor; no local or activity-based scoring; no online or continual setting; no per-neuron budgets; no learning-time gradual pruning.

title: Topology optimization of random memristors for input-aware dynamic SNN
authors: Bo Wang, Xinyuan Zhang, Shaocong Wang, et al. (18 authors in Crossref; arXiv v1 lists 15, incl. Zhongrui Wang and Dashan Shang as corresponding)
venue: Science Advances 11(16), 18 Apr 2025 (first public as arXiv preprint, cs.ET, 26 Jul 2024)
claim: PRIME applies pruning-based topology optimization to a random memristive spiking network, without fine-tuning conductances. Pop-up (edge-popup) scores are updated on a digital processor by backprop with a straight-through estimator. An input-aware early-stop policy adds runtime savings. On a 40 nm, 256 Kb memristor macro, classification accuracy and Inception Score are comparable to the software baseline. Energy efficiency improves 37.83x and 62.50x over digital baselines, and computational load drops 77.0% and 12.5%.
check: All claimed points are confirmed in the arXiv v1 full text and the Crossref abstract. Methods: "On the backward pass, the general digital processor calculates the loss function's gradients to optimize the scores... The pop-up score is updated using the straight-through estimator." Abstract: "optimizes the topology of a random memristive SNN, without expensive memristor conductance fine-tuning". It also reports "40 nm 256 Kb memristor-based in-memory computing macro", "37.83x and 62.50x improvements in energy efficiency" and "77.0% and 12.5% computational load savings". Top-k% pop-up-score masking is edge-popup-style. The paper itself does not use the name 'edge-popup'.
relevance: A second case of pruning-as-learning on memristor hardware, this time covering the 'spiking + subtractive + analog' corner. The same caveat applies: mask learning is BP-based and offline, so a BP-free, online, activity-driven pruning rule would still be new.

title: Pruning for Improved ADC Efficiency in Crossbar-based Analog In-memory Accelerators
authors: Timur Ibrayev, Isha Garg, Indranil Chakraborty, Kaushik Roy (Purdue)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.ET), v1 19 Mar 2024
claim: ADCs take a significant share of crossbar energy and area. When one ADC is shared by a tile's columns, its precision is set by the least sparse column, and sparsity helps only at discrete levels (50% removes 1 bit, 75% removes 2 bits). The paper proposes D.U.B. sparsity (discrete, unstructured, balanced across columns), induced by regularizing the variance of column L0 norms. Results: up to 7.13x (CIFAR-10) and 1.27x (ImageNet) ADC-energy improvement with under 1% accuracy drop. On VGG11 with 64x64 tiles, D.U.B. gave 4x, versus 2.6x for plain unstructured pruning, 3.1x for row pruning, 3.53x for tile pruning and 2.43x for column pruning.
check: Full text (pdftotext of v1) supports every claim. Sec. III: "within a tile, we assume that an ADC is shared between all columns... precision is dictated... only by the sparsity of the least sparse column"; 50% sparsity = 1 bit, 75% = 2 bits. Method: variance of column L0 norms regularized, with gradient gating, plus per-tile pruning. Abstract gives 7.13x (CIFAR-10) and 1.27x (ImageNet) with under 1% accuracy drop. Table I (VGG11, 64x64): 4x vs 2.6x unstructured, 3.1x row, 3.53x tile, 2.43x column pruning, all matching.
relevance: Direct counter-evidence for moving our hub allocation to crossbars. A crossbar column is a receiving neuron, so activity-proportional per-neuron budgets mean deliberately unbalanced column sparsity. The dense hub columns then set the ADC resolution, so ADC energy barely drops. A crossbar version would need per-column ADC resolution or hubs packed into separate tiles. Related: Xue et al., DATE 2023 (DOI:10.23919/date56975.2023.10136975), hierarchical non-structured pruning for lower ADC resolution.

title: PIM-Prune: Fine-Grain DCNN Pruning for Crossbar-Based Process-In-Memory Architecture
authors: Chaoqun Chu, Yanzhi Wang, Yilong Zhao, Xiaolong Ma, Shaokai Ye, Yunyan Hong, Xiaoyao Liang, Yinhe Han, Li Jiang (9 authors)
venue: 2020 57th ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), July 2020
claim: Exploiting weight sparsity on crossbar PIM is nontrivial because of the crossbar structure. Coarse filter- or channel-level pruning fits crossbars but costs accuracy. Finer-grained, crossbar-aware pruning reduces the number of occupied crossbars: for ResNet18, up to 24.85x (CIFAR-10) and 3.56x (ImageNet) higher crossbar compression with negligible accuracy loss. Smaller crossbars suit pruning better, but their peripheral circuits raise power, so each network has an optimal crossbar size.
check: The abstract (Crossrefs/OpenAlex) supports every point. It says coarse filter/channel pruning fits crossbars but "inevitably degrades the model accuracy". Its result: "up to 24.85x and 3.56x higher compression rate of occupied crossbars on Cifar10 and Imagenet" for ResNet18, with negligible accuracy loss. It also says smaller crossbars suit pruning better but "the resulting peripheral circuit cause higher power consumption". Its "sweet-spot of crossbar design" per DCNN matches the claimed optimal crossbar size. The abstract also says the result is 4.56x and 1.99x better than state-of-the-art methods. The secondary reference is real: Lin et al., "Learning the sparsity for ReRAM", ASP-DAC 2019, DOI 10.1145/3287624.3287715. Its abstract reports "3 -- 5X energy efficiency and more than 2.5 -- 6X speedup" over dense accelerators, using crossbar-grained pruning plus sparse mapping.
relevance: Defines what sparsity actually saves on a crossbar: freed crossbars, tiles and periphery, not nonzero weights. Our Wanda-style and hub-allocation results would have to be re-scored as crossbars freed after mapping. Similar result: Lin et al., ASP-DAC 2019 (DOI:10.1145/3287624.3287715) report 3-5x energy efficiency and 2.5-6x speedup from crossbar-grained pruning versus dense mapping.

title: TraNNsformer: Neural network transformation for memristive crossbar based neuromorphic system design
authors: Aayush Ankit, Abhronil Sengupta, Kaushik Roy
venue: 2017 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD), pp. 533-540; preprint arXiv:1708.07949 (26 Aug 2017)
claim: Plain network pruning produces irregular connections 'incoherent to the crossbar structure', which gives highly inefficient area and energy. Iterating prune, cluster and retrain to form crossbar-sized clusters cut area by 28-55% and energy by 49-67% versus the original MLP-SNNs (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10) without accuracy loss. Against plain pruning, it still saved 28-49% area and 15-29% energy.
check: Abstract (via OpenAlex): pruning "induce[s] irregular connections that are incoherent to the crossbar structure"; "reduces the area (energy) consumption by 28%-55% (49%-67%)"; vs pruning "28%-49% (15%-29%) area (energy) savings". MLP-SNNs on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10, without accuracy loss. All numbers and method (iterative prune + cluster + retrain) match.
relevance: Quantifies the penalty for unstructured pruning on memristive crossbars. An emulator scoreboard must include a mapping or clustering step, otherwise pruned weights still occupy cells and ADC columns. Hub allocation would need such a clustering stage before it could pay off.

title: Long Live TIME: Improving Lifetime for Training-In-Memory Engines by Structured Gradient Sparsification
authors: Yi Cai, Lin, Xia, Chen, Han, Wang, Yang (7 authors; Crossref family names)
venue: 2018 55th ACM/ESDA/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), June 2018; extended as 'Long Live TIME: Improving Lifetime and Security for NVM-Based Training-in-Memory Systems', IEEE TCAD, Dec 2020, DOI:10.1109/tcad.2020.2977079
claim: RRAM endurance limits training-in-memory because weights are rewritten thousands to millions of times during training. Ordinary gradient sparsification spreads writes unevenly. Structured gradient sparsification plus aging-aware row swapping (SGS-ARS) balances writes across crossbars and extends lifetime 356x when training ResNet-50 on ImageNet. The TCAD version also shows BP lets an attacker wear out targeted cells and recovers an 84x lifetime gain under attack.
check: Both abstracts (OpenAlex) support the claims. DAC: "356x lifetime extension is achieved when TIME is programmed to train ResNet-50 on Imagenet dataset with our SGS-ARS framework." TCAD: "conventional GS will introduce nonuniform writes on different cells" and "Under the adversarial environment, the available lifetime ... can still be improved by 84x". TCAD also says BP "allows the attacker to localize and update fixed memory locations and wear them out" (defenses: Random-ARS + Refresh). Minor nuance: the DAC abstract's complaint about plain gradient sparsification is "unacceptable computation cost"; the uneven-writes framing comes from the TCAD abstract.
relevance: Establishes device writes and endurance as a legitimate scoreboard axis where sparse or subtractive updates pay off on analog hardware but not on GPUs. A candidate positive result for us is writes per unit of accuracy in online learning. Sparsified or thresholded BP (TIME; Nandakumar mixed precision) must then be a baseline, not naive per-step BP.

title: DNN+NeuroSim V2.0: An End-to-End Benchmarking Framework for Compute-in-Memory Accelerators for On-Chip Training
authors: Xiaochen Peng, Shanshi Huang, Hongwu Jiang, Anni Lu, Shimeng Yu
venue: arXiv preprint 2020; published IEEE TCAD vol. 40, pp. 2306-2319, Nov 2021
claim: A PyTorch-wrapped circuit-level estimator of area, latency, energy and accuracy for on-chip training on SRAM and eNVM CIM, modelling update nonlinearity, asymmetry, and device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variation. For VGG-8 on CIFAR-10: the 6-bit ADC dominates area, and buffer latency plus DRAM energy are the bottleneck. Weight-gradient computation dominates latency and energy, because it runs in SRAM-CIM with activations and errors loaded from off-chip and frequent SRAM writes. Weight-update latency and energy are negligible because they are amortized over batch size 200. Forward and error passes cost about the same, via transposable arrays. Recommended device specs: C2C variation under 1%, Ron above 100 kOhm, write pulses under 1 us, nonlinearity within +/-3. At 7 nm, parallel-read SRAM CIM still has better energy efficiency and throughput.
check: Full text checks out. The breakdown is for the FeFET-based design at epoch 100: "the 6-bit ADC ... is dominant in the total area"; "the buffer latency and DRAM energy are the bottleneck". Weight-gradient computation dominates because of off-chip loads and SRAM-CIM writes. "the batch size is 200 ... latency and energy of weight update are averaged by 200x". Forward and error passes are similar via transposable arrays. Specs: "low cycle-to-cycle variation (<1%), large on-state resistance (>100 k), small write pulse width (<1s), with nonlinearity below +3/-3". At 7 nm, parallel-read SRAM has "superior energy efficiency and throughput".
relevance: The only open tool found that reports energy, latency and area breakdowns for training: GitHub neurosim/DNN_NeuroSim_V2.1, last commit 2024-02, Linux install, one cell per synapse, about 12 h per VGG-8 run. Its accounting says data movement and gradient computation dominate, not the array, so BP-free rules win only if they change that traffic. Key point for our online continual setting: at batch size 1, update and write energy is not amortized (200x more per sample than in this benchmark). That is where local, sparse or subtractive updates could matter, and no paper found quantifies it.

title: Multiscale Co-Design Analysis of Energy, Latency, Area, and Accuracy of a ReRAM Analog Neural Training Accelerator
authors: Matthew J. Marinella, Sapan Agarwal, Alexander Hsia, Isaac Richter, Robin Jacobs-Gedrim, John Niroula, Steven J. Plimpton, Engin Ipek, Conrad D. James (9 authors)
venue: IEEE JETCAS vol. 8, pp. 86-101 (March 2018); arXiv preprint July 2017
claim: Detailed 14/16 nm circuit and device design of an analog ReRAM crossbar block for the three training kernels: VMM, transposed MVM, and parallel rank-1 outer-product update. It takes about 11 fJ per MAC. Versus digital ReRAM, it has a 270x energy and 540x latency advantage; versus SRAM, 430x energy and 34x latency. The text states that the ADC and integrator dominate the analog block's energy. Training accuracy is degraded by device nonidealities. Analysis is at the kernel level; a full accelerator architecture is left to future work.
check: Full text read. The abstract says "270x energy and 540x latency advantage over a similar block utilizing only digital ReRAM and takes only 11 fJ per multiply and accumulate (MAC)". It also gives 430X energy and 34X latency versus SRAM. The three kernels are VMM, transpose MVM and rank-1 outer-product update, on a 14/16 nm PDK. Sec. II text: "The ADC and integrator still dominate the energy". Discussion: "These improvements are at the kernel level, a full accelerator architecture must be developed". Training accuracy is degraded by write nonidealities (nonlinearity, asymmetry, stochasticity).
relevance: Shows that transposed reads and outer-product updates are natively cheap in the array, so BP is not handicapped on AIMC at kernel level. Periphery (ADC/integrator) is the cost driver, so the scoreboard should count ADC conversions per learning step. A BP-free rule that skips the transposed MVM saves one of the three ADC-heavy kernels per step, which is a modest but honest upper bound on its kernel-level advantage.

title: Acceleration of Deep Neural Network Training with Resistive Cross-Point Devices: Design Considerations
authors: Tayfun Gokmen, Yurii Vlasov (IBM T.J. Watson)
venue: Frontiers in Neuroscience 10:333 (published online 2016-07-21); arXiv preprint March 2016
claim: Introduces the resistive processing unit (RPU). On a crossbar, forward and backward (transposed) vector-matrix products are O(1); the local parallel weight update uses stochastic pulse coincidence (an AND at each cross-point), which makes the outer-product update O(1) as well. Projections for about 1B-weight DNNs: 30,000x acceleration over microprocessors and 84,000 GigaOps/s/W. ADCs (4096 per tile) dominate tile area and power, so time-multiplexing is needed. Up/down conductance asymmetry is the most restrictive device spec: changes must be balanced within about 5%.
check: Full text (arXiv PDF) checked. All claims hold. Backward pass: "when voltage pulses are supplied from columns ... the vector-matrix product is computed on the transpose of a matrix". Update: "the multiplication operation can be reduced to a simple AND operation", done through pulse coincidence, which gives O(1) update time. Abstract: "about 1 billion weights ... acceleration factors of 30,000 ... power efficiency of 84,000 [GigaOps/s/W]". ADCs: "dominated by the contribution from 4096 ADC". The paper then time-multiplexes them, with each ADC shared by 64 columns. Asymmetry: up and down changes "need to be significantly balanced (within 5% of the mean)" to reach a 0.3% error penalty.
relevance: This is the core reason BP also 'plays at home' on resistive crossbars: the weight-transport problem is solved physically by reading the same array transposed, and the outer-product update is local and parallel. The user's premise that non-von-Neumann substrates handicap BP therefore does not hold for AIMC crossbars as such. BP's remaining costs are the ADC'd backward pass, activation storage, and sensitivity to update asymmetry, so a BP-free advantage must be argued on those.

title: Mixed-Precision Deep Learning Based on Computational Memory
authors: S. R. Nandakumar, Manuel Le Gallo, et al. (14 authors, per Crossref)
venue: Frontiers in Neuroscience 14:406 (published 2020-05-12); arXiv preprint v1 submitted 31 Jan 2020
claim: A PCM crossbar performs the weighted sums and imprecise conductance updates, while a digital unit accumulates weight updates in high precision. A hardware/software MLP experiment on MNIST reached 97.73%, within 0.6% of software. With PCM models, CNNs, LSTMs and GANs reach floating-point-comparable accuracy. A system-level study gives 172x energy efficiency (173x in arXiv v1) for MLP training versus a dedicated fully digital 32-bit implementation.
check: Abstract: "a computational memory unit performing the weighted summations and imprecise conductance updates with a digital processing unit that accumulates the weight updates in high precision" ... "97.73% test accuracy ... within 0.6% of the software baseline". arXiv v1 says 173x and Frontiers says 172x energy efficiency vs a 32-bit digital design. The full text confirms thresholding: "When the magnitude of χ exceeds ε (= 0.096 ...)" a single pulse is applied, which gives ">three orders of magnitude reduction in the number of updates".
relevance: Mixed precision is the practical analog-BP baseline; AIHWKit has mixed-precision presets. Its digital accumulator already reduces device writes, because a device is programmed only after the accumulated update is large enough. Any write-count advantage claimed for local or pruning rules must be measured against this thresholded BP. It also shows gradient-related traffic stays in digital, which is the cost local rules might avoid.

title: Making Analog Training Scale: Co-Designing Mapping, Optimizer, and Converters
authors: Zhaoxian Wu, Tayfun Gokmen, Omobayode Fagbohungbe, T. Patrick Xiao, Tianyi Chen
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG; cs.AR), v1 29 Sep 2026
claim: Mixed-precision AIMC training: forward and backward MVMs run in analog, weight gradients in digital. The system co-optimizes weight mapping for well-conditioned physical and logical weights, a preconditioned optimizer with threshold-triggered open-loop pulsing, and ADC/DAC dynamic-range alignment. In architectural simulations calibrated on electrochemical RAM measurements, it trains Transformers up to 123M parameters. Validation loss scales as L ~ N^-0.231, versus N^-0.238 for digital training.
check: Abstract and full text support every point: "executing forward and backward matrix multiplications in the analog domain while computing weight gradients in the digital domain". The co-design covers mapping, a preconditioned optimizer with threshold-triggered open-loop pulsing, and converter range alignment. Scaling reaches 123M parameters, with L ∝ N^-0.231 for analog versus N^-0.238 for digital AdamW.
relevance: State of the art as of Sept 2026: analog BP now scales to 100M+ parameter Transformers, so 'BP cannot run on AIMC' is not a viable premise. It also confirms the field moved gradient computation back to digital, which brings back activation and error movement (cf. Wolters: about 95% of energy in off-chip buffers). That traffic is precisely the cost a local rule with in-array updates could avoid. Converter range and precision are named as first-class training costs.

title: Using the IBM analog in-memory hardware acceleration kit for neural network training and inference
authors: Manuel Le Gallo, Corey Lammie, Julian Büchel, Fabio Carta, Omobayode Fagbohungbe, Charles Mackin, Hsinyu Tsai, Vijay Narayanan, Abu Sebastian, Kaoutar El Maghraoui, Malte J. Rasch (11 authors)
venue: APL Machine Learning 1(4):041102 (published 2023-11-28, CC BY 4.0); arXiv cs.ET, v1 July 2023, v2 26 Jan 2024
claim: Tutorial and best practices for AIHWKit. It provides PyTorch analog layers and a CUDA-capable C++ tile simulator. The simulator models output noise, ADC/DAC discretization and bounds, stochastic update pulse trains with a finite step per coincidence, D2D/C2C variation and asymmetry, and device presets calibrated to hardware. Training options are in-situ analog training (SGD and the Tiki-Taka family; the CHANGELOG adds ChoppedTTv2, AGAD and mixed-precision presets) and hardware-aware training for inference. It also covers the Analog AI Cloud Composer.
check: The metadata matches Crossref (title, 11 authors, APL ML vol 1, issue 4, article 041102). The full text (arXiv v2 via pdftotext) supports each content claim. It has a RpuCuda tile in C++/CUDA. Its MVM nonidealities are output noise ("0.04 Standard deviation of Gaussian output noise"), ADC/DAC discretization, and noise/bound management. Device updates are explicit per pulse: "each single incremental pulse update is explicitly modelled according to a device response model". It models d2d and pulse-to-pulse variation, and its device presets are "set according to measurements" (ReRAM, ECRAM, CMOS, PCM). It covers HWA training and the Analog AI Cloud Composer. On training it says: "in-memory SGD using stochastic pulse trains ... Mixedprecision, Tiki-taka I & II ... Chopped-TTv2 (c-TTv2) and ... AGAD" (Tab. IX). The paper also directly supports limit (1): AIHWKit "is a functional simulator that aims to compute the attainable accuracy ... and is not concerned with performance or latency estimation".
relevance: The practical emulator for running our learners on AIMC: analog tiles replace nn.Linear/Conv, so BP and Tiki-Taka baselines run as-is, and custom DFA or NP updates can be injected through the tile update. Limits we verified: (1) the README lists accuracy and noise features but no energy or latency model, so energy must come from NeuroSim or our own pulse/ADC-count model, kept as a model-based estimate per the project rule. (2) PyPI aihwkit 1.1.0 (2026-02-10) ships only manylinux and macOS wheels, with no win_amd64; conda is supported only on Linux/WSL. That means the RunPod Linux pod, which needs the user's OK. (3) aihwkit-lightning 2.1.0 is pure Python but pins torch==2.13.0 (our venv has 2.11) and targets hardware-aware training for inference.

title: Budgeted Broadcast: An Activity-Dependent Pruning Rule for Neural Network Efficiency
authors: Yaron Meirovitch, Fuming Yang, Jeff W. Lichtman, Nir Shavit
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG), v1 26 Sep 2025
claim: Gives each unit a local traffic budget: long-term on-rate a_i times fan-out k_i. A constrained-entropy analysis yields the balance log((1-a_i)/a_i) = beta*k_i. Local actuators enforce it by pruning either fan-in (to lower activity) or fan-out (to reduce broadcast). At matched sparsity it improves accuracy for Transformers (ASR), ResNets (face identification) and 3D U-Nets (EM synapse prediction), sometimes beating dense baselines.
check: Full PDF read. Abstract: "gives each unit a local traffic budget--the product of its long-term on-rate and fan-out"; "local actuators that prune either fan-in (to lower activity) or fan-out (to reduce broadcast)"; "improves accuracy at matched sparsity across Transformers for ASR, ResNets for face identification, and 3D U-Nets for synapse prediction, sometimes exceeding dense baselines." The balance is log((1-a)/a) proportional to k, derived from a Lagrangian under a total traffic budget. The Greek constant did not survive pdftotext, so the symbol "beta" in the scout's record could not be checked. It is likely the Lagrange multiplier. Section 2 says hardware patterns are out of scope: "our focus is on the allocation principle rather than the implementation pattern". So the claim of no hardware cost model holds.
relevance: Novelty threat to hub allocation itself, regardless of emulator: activity-dependent per-unit connection budgets for pruning were published in 2025. The direction differs. Budgeted Broadcast trims the fan-out of high-activity units, while hub allocation gives more fan-in to high-activity receivers, so the two must be compared head-to-head. It has no hardware cost model. Its fan-out actuator maps naturally to emptying crossbar rows, and its fan-in actuator to emptying columns.

title: STDP-Based Pruning of Connections and Weight Quantization in Spiking Neural Networks for Energy-Efficient Recognition
authors: Nitin Rathi, Priyadarshini Panda, Kaushik Roy
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems, vol. 38, no. 4, pp. 668-677 (April 2019); arXiv preprint submitted 12 Oct 2017
claim: At regular intervals during SNN training, prunes synapses whose pre- and post-synaptic spiking is weakly correlated (power-law weight-dependent STDP). Surviving weights are quantized to the available conductance levels so the network fits crossbar size and power budget. Results: MNIST 90.1% (Caltech-101 subset 91.6%), with 3.1x (2.2x) energy and 4x (2.6x) area improvement over the unpruned 2-layer fully connected SNN.
check: The abstract and the full text support every number and method detail. Abstract: "achieved a classification accuracy of 90.1% (91.6%) on the MNIST (Caltech-101) dataset with 3.1x (2.2x) and 4x (2.6x) improvement in energy and area." The baseline is the unpruned 2-layer fully connected SNN ("The fully connected topology serves as the baseline design"). Pruning and quantization to the available conductance levels happen "at regular intervals during training." One nuance on mechanism: the paper calls it spike-correlation pruning, but the actual criterion is the weight learned by STDP. Synapses whose weight is below a fixed pruning threshold are set to zero after each batch, and they can become critical again later. They are removed permanently only after the final batch.
relevance: Precedent for activity-driven pruning during training, aimed at crossbar energy and area, so 'activity-based pruning for crossbars' is not new by itself. Still new: neuron-level budgets proportional to postsynaptic activity, the tile-emptying analysis, and evaluation under realistic device noise in a modern simulator.

title: Examining and Mitigating the Impact of Crossbar Non-idealities for Accurate Implementation of Sparse Deep Neural Networks
authors: Abhiroop Bhattacharjee, Lakshya Bhatnagar, Priyadarshini Panda
venue: DATE 2022 (Design, Automation & Test in Europe), arXiv v1 posted 13 Jan 2022
claim: The paper uses a PyTorch crossbar simulator. It models interconnect parasitic resistances plus Gaussian synaptic variation and non-linearity. VGG11/CIFAR10 was structure-pruned at s=0.8. C/F pruning gives 19.69x crossbar compression on 32x32 crossbars. On 64x64 crossbars, accuracy dropped versus software by about 39% (C/F), 24% (XCS) and 30% (XRS); the unpruned model dropped about 21%. Lower sparsity (s=0.5) reduced the drop. Crossbar column rearrangement improved C/F-pruned accuracy by about 9% (VGG11, 64x64) and about 6% (VGG16, 32x32) on CIFAR10. Weight-constrained training made the pruned net about 6% (CIFAR10, 64x64) and about 7% (CIFAR100 at s=0.6, 32x32) more accurate than the unpruned model. For VGG16/CIFAR10 on 64x64 crossbars, the C/F-pruned net beat the unpruned one because the unpruned net needs more crossbars and its NF rises faster.
check: The paper exists, and the full text (pdftotext) supports the main finding. Quote from Sec. V: "on 64×64 crossbars, the inference accuracy of the unpruned model reduces by ~21% ... C/F pruning, XCS and XRS, the decline is ~39%, ~24% and ~30%". Five points need fixing. (1) The 19.69x crossbar-compression figure (VGG11/CIFAR10, C/F, s=0.8) is for 32x32 crossbars (Table I), not 64x64. (2) The simulator does more than model circuit parasitics (Rdriver, Rwire, Rsense). It also models synaptic variation and non-linearity using Gaussian profiling. (3) The mitigation numbers are mixed up. Column rearrangement (R) gave about 9% for VGG11 on 64x64 and about 6% for VGG16 on 32x32 (CIFAR10). The WCT figures of about 6% (CIFAR10, 64x64) and about 7% (CIFAR100, 32x32) are the WCT-DNN's lead over the unpruned model. They are not an amount "recovered". (4) CIFAR100 experiments use s=0.6, not 0.8. (5) The VGG16 64x64 result (C/F-pruned beats unpruned) is correct. The paper explains it by the unpruned net needing more crossbars, so its NF rises faster from 32x32 to 64x64.
relevance: Counter-evidence for C1. High sparsity leaves fewer, larger-conductance weights, and these are more exposed to IR-drop-type non-idealities. An extreme-sparsity hub network (1-10% density) may therefore lose its accuracy edge on a crossbar, and dense hub columns carrying large weights may be hit hardest. A positive C1 claim needs results with noise switched on, using these mitigations as baselines.

title: Design Space Exploration of Dense and Sparse Mapping Schemes for RRAM Architectures
authors: Corey Lammie, Jason K. Eshraghian, Chenqi Li, Amirali Amirsoleimani, Roman Genov, Wei D. Lu, Mostafa Rahimi Azghadi
claim: This is a DSE methodology for RRAM crossbar accelerators running inference with pre-trained CNNs. It compares dense and sparse (staggered) kernel-to-crossbar mapping schemes by device count and read/write operations, which is a layout question, not weight pruning. Its CIFAR-10 case study sweeps tile size, batch size and bit-width under simulated 1T1R non-idealities and finds that tiles of about 64 work best, with the best size depending on the architecture. The abstract speculates ("may be") that sparse connectivity is more noise-susceptible because of under-parameterization, but the paper presents no experiment that isolates this. It is a weak counter-signal at best for pruning-under-noise. It is still useful as a template for sweeping tile size x bit-width x non-ideality.
check: Metadata confirmed (Crossref + arXiv). The abstract does contain the hedged sentence: "its performance on tiled RRAM arrays may be more susceptible to noise due to under-parameterization, when compared to dense mapping schemes." But in this paper "sparse mapping" means a staggered/sparse LAYOUT of convolution kernels on crossbars (Fig. 1c vs 1d, plus differential-interconnect rerouting from [7]). It does not mean pruned or sparse weights. The body never tests the noise claim. Table II reports one test accuracy per architecture and bit-width that all mapping schemes share. The schemes differ only in required devices and read/write operations, folded into a score of TSA/(RD x RWO). The case study sweeps tile size, batch size and bit-width (4/6/8) for VGG-16, ResNeXt29, MobileNetV2 and GoogLeNet on CIFAR-10 with fixed-seed non-idealities. Its main finding is that tiles of about 64 were optimal and that the best tile size depends on the architecture and the bit-width.
relevance: A second, independent counter-signal. It also offers a ready-made evaluation template for C1: sweep sparsity x tile size x non-ideality. It reinforces that the scoreboard must include accuracy under device noise, not just the number of emptied tiles.

title: Fast offset corrected in-memory training (arXiv v1); published as "Fast and robust analog in-memory deep neural network training"
authors: Malte J. Rasch, Fabio Carta, Omebayode Fagbohungbe, Tayfun Gokmen
venue: arXiv preprint 2023-03-08; Nature Communications, published 2024-08-20
claim: Introduces Chopped-TTv2 (c-TTv2) and AGAD, in-memory training algorithms from the Tiki-Taka family. They keep the runtime complexity of TTv2 but correct remaining offsets with choppers, which greatly relaxes the device requirements for fast in-memory DNN training.
check: Abstract: proposes "Chopped-TTv2 (c-TTv2) and Analog Gradient Accumulation with Dynamic reference (AGAD), that retain the same runtime complexity but correct for any remaining offsets using choppers... greatly relax the device requirements". Matches the claimed content.
relevance: These are the analog-backprop baselines C2 must beat. They are available in IBM aihwkit (arXiv 2104.02184; tutorial arXiv 2307.09357). Wu et al. 2024 (arXiv 2406.12774) prove that plain analog SGD on asymmetric devices keeps a non-vanishing asymptotic error, while Tiki-Taka converges exactly, so beating plain analog SGD would be a strawman. Backprop is not handicapped on crossbars per se: forward pass, backward pass and rank-1 outer-product updates all run array-parallel. Node perturbation's update is also a rank-1 outer product (perturbation x input) and can reuse the same pulse-coincidence update hardware. Any advantage must therefore come from skipping the backward pass and from noise tolerance, not from cheaper updates.

title: Node perturbation can effectively train multi-layer neural networks
authors: Sander Dalm, Marcel van Gerven, Nasir Ahmad
venue: arXiv preprint (Oct 2023, v8 Jun 2026); published in Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering, vol. 6, no. 3 (2026), IOP
claim: Reframes node perturbation (activity-perturbed forward gradients) as a directional derivative and adds layer-wise input decorrelation. This greatly improves parameter convergence and test performance, approaching backprop. The formulation also trains noisy systems whose noise process is not accessible, which the authors note is relevant to on-chip neuromorphic learning.
check: The abstract supports the claim: "relating it to the directional derivative and incorporating input decorrelation ... much higher performance on the test data, approaching that of BP." It also says the method applies "to noisy systems in which the noise process itself is inaccessible ... on-chip learning in neuromorphic systems." Section 3 trains with two noisy passes and no clean pass.
relevance: Supports C2. The project's NP results (11-14% A_AUC on Split CIFAR-10, divergence without weight decay) probably reflect vanilla NP. A decorrelated NP is the fair learner to port into an analog simulator. The 'inaccessible noise' formulation suggests intrinsic device or read noise could act as the perturbation source. A related forward-only method for physical NNs is FFzero (arXiv 2603.24790, tested on a simulated photonic NN). Neither has been evaluated inside an IMC simulator, so that remains open.

title: Stochastic Sparse Learning with Momentum Adaptation for Imprecise Memristor Networks
authors: Yaoyuan Wang, Shuang Wu, Ziyang Zhang, Lei Tian, Luping Shi (Tsinghua)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.ET), v1 6 Jun 2019; no journal version found via Crossref
claim: SSM (a simulation study) trains imprecise memristor networks in situ with stochastic, discrete, sparse updates, momentum, re-initialization against D2D variation, and an optional update compensation. Without compensation, accuracy rises from 26.12% to 87.18% (MLP, MNIST) and from 65.98% to 90.99% (CNN, Fashion-MNIST). Programming pulses drop 90% / 40% (counted over the first 5 epochs), and convergence is 3x faster. With compensation, accuracy reaches 90.07% / 92.38%, but the pulse count goes back to roughly the no-SSM baseline and extra reads are needed. The write-frugality point still holds: fewer than 1% of cells are updated per iteration. The write-saving and best-accuracy figures should not be quoted as one combined result.
check: The abstract numbers match (26.12->90.07 MLP, 65.98->92.38 CNN, pulses -90%/-40%, 3x faster). But the body splits the two results: "the classification accuracy increases from 26.12% to 87.18% in MLP, and the programming pulse number in the first 5 epochs decreases 90%" (CNN: 90.99%, -40%). With compensation (90.07/92.38), "the pulse number still approximates to that without the SSM scheme". So the best accuracy and the pulse savings do not happen together. All results come from device-model simulation (MNIST MLP, Fashion-MNIST CNN), not hardware.
relevance: Counter-evidence to the hope that perturbation wins 'per device write'. Gradient-based in-situ training can already be made write-frugal with sparse stochastic updates. A C2 write-count comparison must therefore include sparse-update backprop baselines, not only dense analog SGD.

title: Local rules for fabricating allosteric networks
authors: Nidhi Pashine (sole author, University of Chicago)
venue: Physical Review Materials 5, 065607 (published 2021-06-28); arXiv v1 2021-01-17 (cond-mat.soft)
claim: Creates a long-range allosteric response in disordered networks by pruning bonds in situ, deciding which bond to prune from local stresses only, with no global cost function. Designs are made in simulation and then built from real materials. Some local pruning strategies transfer to experiment better than others. The paper also gives a method to measure local stresses experimentally.
check: The abstract supports every point. It prunes "based purely on the local stresses in the network without employing a cost function". Designs are made "in simulations and then built out of real materials". It reports that "some pruning strategies work better than others when translated into an experimental system". It also presents "a method ... to measure local stresses experimentally". The target is one long-range allosteric (input strain to output strain) response, not supervised learning from data. That matches the scout's framing.
relevance: Direct precedent for learning by permanent, locally decided edge removal in a physical network. The subtractive half of C3 therefore exists, but for designing one target response, not for data-driven supervised learning. Earlier global-greedy versions: Goodrich et al. 2015, 'tuning by pruning' (PRL, DOI 10.1103/physrevlett.114.225501), and Rocks et al. 2019, limits of multifunctionality by adding and removing links in flow and mechanical networks (PNAS, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1806790116). Still open: combining coupled learning or EP (continuous conductance adaptation) with local-rule edge removal on supervised tasks, scored by accuracy versus power and edge count.

title: Equilibrium Propagation for Complete Directed Neural Networks
authors: Matilde Tristany Farinha, Sérgio Pequito, Pedro A. Santos, Mário A. T. Figueiredo
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG)
claim: Extends equilibrium propagation to complete directed networks. Contributions: new neuronal dynamics and learning rule, a sparsity-inducing method that can prune irrelevant connections, and a Lyapunov-based characterization.
check: The abstract states it directly: "we introduce: a new neuronal dynamics and learning rule for arbitrary network architectures; a sparsity-inducing method able to prune irrelevant connections; a dynamical-systems characterization ... using Lyapunov theory." The full text names the framework DEEP (DirEcted EP), which allows asymmetric weights. Pruning comes from L1 regularization in the learning rule plus sparsity enforced at each weight update.
relevance: 'EP plus connection pruning' exists for abstract neural networks. It does not exist for Kirchhoff-constrained resistor or flow networks with power metrics, or with a local, physically measurable pruning signal. That is the space C3 still has.

title: Microscopic Imprints of Learned Solutions in Tunable Networks (arXiv v1 title: "Microscopic imprints of learned solutions in adaptive resistor networks")
authors: Marcel Guzman, Felipe Martins, Menachem Stern, Andrea J. Liu
venue: Physical Review X 15, 031056 (published 2025-08-27); arXiv preprint 2024-12-26
claim: In contrastive local-learning resistor networks, all physical information about the trained input-output relation is captured by a susceptibility, which can be measured experimentally. Simulations show susceptibility correlates positively with an edge's functional importance.
check: Abstract supports the claim: "all the physical information relevant to the trained input-output relation can be captured by a susceptibility, an experimentally measurable quantity" and simulations show "the susceptibility is positively correlated with functional importance". Setting is electrical contrastive local learning resistor networks, matching the claim.
relevance: Gives a physically measurable edge-importance signal, which is a natural local pruning criterion for C3 that needs no digital model. No paper found uses it to remove edges during learning. Also relevant: Lin et al. 2026 (arXiv 2602.03546) report little degradation when only a subset of resistances is updated, and Kim et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.09756) give a general perturbative-contrast learning framework demonstrated on spring networks and photonic circuits.

title: Dependence of Equilibrium Propagation Training Success on Network Architecture
authors: Qingshan Wang, Clara C. Wanjura, Florian Marquardt
venue: arXiv preprint
claim: Trains XY-model networks with equilibrium propagation and finds that sparse, locally connected lattices perform comparably to dense networks on benchmark tasks.
check: Abstract: "We train an XY model ... Our results show that sparse networks with only local connections can achieve performance comparable to dense networks." Claim matches; sparsity is architectural (locally connected lattices), not reached by pruning.
relevance: Supports C3's premise that physical learning tolerates sparse, local connectivity, which is a prerequisite for pruning to high sparsity. However, the sparsity here is fixed by design, not reached by pruning during learning.

title: A flexible framework for structural plasticity in GPU-accelerated sparse spiking neural networks
authors: James C. Knight, Johanna Senk, Thomas Nowotny
venue: arXiv cs.NE (Oct 2025; v2 23 Jan 2026); published Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering 6(1), 2026 (IOP, CC-BY)

check: The abstract says: "Compared to baseline dense models, our sparse classifiers reduce training time by up to 10x while the DEEP R rewiring enables them to perform as well as the original models." title: Versatile On-device Adaptation at the Edge by Unifying Few-shot, Zero-shot, Continual, and In-context Learning

venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG), v1 31 Jul 2026; submitted to IEEE

The work runs on the Chameleon SoC at 9.5 uW in real time. The quantized model is 58.2 kB and is 4.4 points below the M5 baseline, which is about 96x larger.

NeuroBench (Yik et al., arXiv 2304.04640) lists Keyword FSCIL among its v1.0 tasks, and per the repository README its metrics include Footprint, ConnectionSparsity, ActivationSparsity and SynapticOperations. venue: IJCAI 2023 (Proceedings of the 32nd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence), pp. Aug 2023; arXiv preprint Aug 2023

check: Abstract (Crossref + arXiv PDF): "dynamically assigns and grows new neurons to new tasks and prunes redundant neurons...
