Related work: DPAP, activity-dependent 'use it or lose it' pruning during learning (arXiv 2211.12714); SAFA-SNN, on-device FSCIL with zeroth-order optimization (arXiv 2510.03648); Mia et al. 2025, GWR-style structural plasticity plus adaptive STDP for lifelong learning, simulated in Lava (arXiv 2508.04610, ICONS 2025).

title: Learning While Inferring: Local and Parallel Learning for Edge SNNs across Sensing Modalities
authors: Yanxun Zhang, Yifei Wang, Changze Lv, ... Xiaoqing Zheng (9 authors)
venue: arXiv preprint (v1 2026-10-02)
claim: Bidirectional Spike-Based Distillation (BSD) couples a stimulus-driven forward SNN with an independent target-driven reverse SNN, aligned through local objectives. Because the two computation graphs stay disjoint until alignment, forward inference, reverse inference and stage-wise updates run concurrently. Across 25 benchmarks in five sensing modalities it stays within 3.8 points of matched backprop on average. It transfers to few-shot class-incremental learning without replay. Projected training latency is 0.72x and estimated training energy 0.36x that of backprop.
check: The abstract supports every claim: "forward inference, reverse inference, and stage-wise updates can run concurrently"; "stays within 3.8 percentage points of matched BP baselines on average"; FSCIL "without replaying past data"; 0.72x projected latency and 0.36x estimated energy. The full text says the latency is a geometric mean over the 25 benchmarks, assumes ideal concurrency, and is below BP on 20 of the 25. The energy figure is an operation-level estimate. Benchmarks span the five modalities of the SOUL benchmark. The word "prun" appears 0 times in the full text. Neuromorphic hardware is mentioned only as background; there is no physical-substrate learning.
relevance: Uses C5's exact framing ('learn while inferring') for edge SNNs, with concurrent updates and inference. It targets digital edge hardware with projected costs and has no pruning and no physical substrate. C5 must cite it and set itself apart through a physical substrate where learning is the physics, plus pruning.

title: Reconfigurable Digital RRAM Logic Enables In-situ Pruning and Learning for Edge AI
authors: Zhongrui Wang (Southern University of Science and Technology; Crossref lists only this author, sequence 'first'; full author list not checked)
venue: Research Square preprint (posted 2025-07-15, not peer reviewed)
claim: Prunes weights in real time during training based on weight similarity, cutting operations by 26.80% on MNIST and 59.94% on ModelNet10 at 91.44% and 77.75% accuracy. The fabricated 180 nm 1T1R RRAM chip is fully digital compute-in-memory with in-memory Boolean logic (no ADC/DAC). It reports 72.30% less area and 57.26% less energy than analog RRAM CIM, and 75.61% / 86.53% less energy than an RTX 4090.
check: The Crossref abstract supports every claimed number: "real-time dynamic weight-pruning strategy that monitors weight similarity during training... reducing operations by 26.80% on MNIST and 59.94% on ModelNet10". It also confirms the rest: 91.44% and 77.75% accuracy, a 180 nm 1T1R fully digital CIM chip with in-memory NAND/AND/XOR/OR logic and no ADC/DAC, and zero bit errors. Against analogue RRAM CIM it cuts area by 72.30% and energy by 57.26%. Against the RTX 4090 it cuts energy by 75.61% (MNIST) and 86.53% (ModelNet10). The brain framing ("simultaneously optimizes synaptic weights and topology... entirely in memory") is also in the abstract.
relevance: Frames 'optimize weights and topology simultaneously, entirely in memory' as the brain principle and implements pruning during learning on in-memory hardware, which overlaps the C5-plus-pruning combination. However, it is digital CIM rather than analog or physical learning, its pruning is similarity-based rather than activity- or hub-based, and it is not peer reviewed.

title: Fully analog end-to-end online training with real-time adaptibility on integrated photonic platform
authors: Zhimu Guo, A. Aadhi, Adam N. McCaughan, Alexander N. Tait, Nathan Youngblood, Sonia M. Buckley, Bhavin J. Shastri
venue: arXiv preprint (physics.optics), v1 22 Jun 2025
claim: A foundry silicon-photonic chip (microring weight bank plus on-chip photodetectors that measure gradient signals) trains in situ, on the fly, with multiplexed gradient descent at gigabaud rates. Classification accuracy exceeds 90% (linear) and 80% (nonlinear). Adaptive online tracking of drifting inputs stays above 90% and is robust to temperature fluctuations and thermal crosstalk.
check: Abstract: "real-time, end-to-end analog training for both linear and nonlinear classification tasks at gigabaud (GBaud) rates, achieving accuracies of over 90% and 80%". It also reports online tracking above 90% and robustness to temperature changes and thermal crosstalk. The foundry silicon-photonic chip, the MRR weight bank with on-chip balanced photodetectors and the use of MGD (perturbative) are all confirmed in the full text.
relevance: The closest hardware demonstration of learning while operating with a perturbative rule on a non-von-Neumann substrate; overlaps C5 and C2. No pruning, and the tasks are tiny. Related: a single-chip photonic DNN trained in situ reached 92.7% on vowel classification, equal to digital (Bandyopadhyay et al., Nature Photonics 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41566-024-01567-z).

title: Lock-in EP: An In-Situ Training Algorithm for Oscillatory Hardware
authors: Sowjanya Tammali, Wilkie Olin-Ammentorp (two authors)
venue: arXiv preprint (v1 submitted 5 Oct 2026)
claim: Lock-in equilibrium propagation (LIEP) gives each component of an oscillatory network local gradient information without separate forward and backward sweeps, enabling in-situ learning on analog oscillatory hardware. It works both for training from scratch and for recovering performance after parameters are perturbed. It can be written as a three-factor rule. So far it is validated only on shallow networks.
check: The abstract supports every claimed point: "LIEP provides local gradient information for each component in an oscillatory network without separate forward and backward sweeps." It also covers ab-initio training, recovery after perturbation, a three-factor update rule, and validation "currently only ... on shallow networks".
relevance: A physical learning rule in which learning and operation share one continuous run with no phase separation, which overlaps C5's 'no separate training phase'. An earlier step is continual EP (Ernoult et al. 2020, arXiv 2005.04168, MNIST), where neuron and synapse dynamics run simultaneously during the nudged phase. Neither includes pruning.

title: On-Chip Error-triggered Learning of Multi-layer Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
authors: Melika Payvand, Mohammed E. Fouda, Fadi Kurdahi, Ahmed M. Eltawil, Emre O. Neftci
venue: IEEE JETCAS 10(4):522-535, Dec 2020 (arXiv first posted 2020-11-21)
claim: A local, gradient-based, error-triggered learning rule with online ternary weight updates trains multi-layer SNNs on memristive crossbar hardware with only a small accuracy loss. The design shares crossbar and peripheral circuits between inference and training (subthreshold, 180 nm). The precursor paper (arXiv:1910.06152, 'Error-triggered Three-Factor Learning Dynamics for Crossbar Arrays') reports that error-triggering cuts the number of weight updates about 100-fold versus the standard rule at on-par accuracy (SPICE plus large-scale simulation, including gesture recognition).
check: The 2011.10852 abstract supports the claim: "local, gradient-based, error-triggered learning algorithm with online ternary weight updates ... multi-layer SNNs with memristive neuromorphic hardware showing a small loss". It also mentions sub-threshold peripheral circuits in 180 nm CMOS. The precursor 1910.06152 abstract says "the number of updates can be reduced hundred-fold compared to the standard rule while achieving performances that are on par", and it reports SPICE on XFAB 180nm plus DVS Gesture. Note that the circuit sharing between inference and training is stated in the precursor's abstract.
relevance: This pre-empts the analog family's 'best honest-positive bet': a local rule on crossbars that needs far fewer device writes per accuracy has already been published, with about 100x fewer writes from event/error gating. Any C2 or write-budget study needs an error-triggered (thresholded) local-rule baseline, and can claim novelty only for the extra write savings from structure (pruning or hub budgets) on top of it.

title: Equivalent-accuracy accelerated neural-network training using analogue memory
authors: Stefano Ambrogio et al. (14 authors, Crossref)
venue: Nature 558, 60-67 (June 2018)
claim: In-situ backprop training on mixed hardware-software implementations of up to 204,900 synapses reached generalization accuracy equivalent to software on MNIST, MNIST-backrand, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Each synapse combines long-term phase-change memory (PCM) storage with a near-linear volatile capacitor, plus 'polarity inversion' to cancel device-to-device variation. The calculated energy efficiency (28,065 GOP/s/W) and throughput per area (3.6 TOP/s/mm^2) exceed those of contemporary GPUs by about two orders of magnitude.
check: The abstract (Europe PMC) supports every number and method detail. Quote: "computational energy efficiency of 28,065 billion operations per second per watt and throughput per area of 3.6 trillion operations per second per square millimetre that we calculate". It also lists up to 204,900 synapses, PCM plus volatile capacitors, 'polarity inversion', and software-equivalent accuracy on MNIST, MNIST-backrand, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
relevance: This directly contradicts the premise that backprop only 'plays at home' on GPUs. On an analog in-memory substrate, BP with a two-timescale (mixed-precision) synapse keeps software accuracy and is projected to be about 100x more efficient than a GPU. So the AIMC scoreboard's BP baseline must be analog BP of this kind (or Tiki-Taka/c-TTv2), not digital BP. The efficiency figure is a calculation, not a measurement.

title: Online Training of Spiking Recurrent Neural Networks with Phase-Change Memory Synapses
authors: Yigit Demirag, Charlotte Frenkel, Melika Payvand, Giacomo Indiveri
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.NE); no journal version found via Crossref/DBLP
claim: Builds a simulation framework for differential-architecture crossbars based on a comprehensive PCM device model and trains a spiking RNN inside it with the local e-prop rule. Implementing the local e-prop updates directly on PCM is hard because of the devices' non-idealities. Of several widely used update schemes compared, gradient accumulation is what enables online, efficient training.
check: Abstract and full text (v2) support the claim. Results: "Out of five configurations, only the mixed-precision approach resulted in an acceptable performance on the pattern generation task (MSE loss < 0.1)". Schemes compared: sign-gradient, stochastic, multi-memristor (N=4, N=8), and mixed-precision (gradients accumulated in double-precision memory, then transferred as pulses). The authors also name the cost: "the mixed-precision scheme comes at the cost of having a high-precision memory that accumulates the updates."
relevance: This is the closest precedent for how C2 is designed: a local rule running inside a device-model crossbar simulator, with update schemes compared. It implies that local rules also need digital gradient accumulation on realistic devices, which weakens the 'no data movement' argument. C2 should run NP/DFA both with and without accumulation (and with a Tiki-Taka-style transfer) and charge the accumulator's memory and energy.

title: L2ight: Enabling On-Chip Learning for Optical Neural Networks via Efficient in-situ Subspace Optimization
authors: Jiaqi Gu, Hanqing Zhu, Chenghao Feng, Zixuan Jiang, Ray T. Chen, David Z. Pan
venue: NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv comment: "Accepted to NeurIPS 2021")
claim: In software simulation with photonic non-idealities, the zeroth-order on-chip protocols FLOPS and MixedTrain handle only toy ONNs of about 2,000 parameters. L2ight (calibration, then mapping of a pretrained model, then in-situ first-order subspace learning with multi-level sparsity) scales more than 1,000x further, to 10M parameters on CIFAR-100/ResNet-18. Where MixedTrain matches its accuracy, L2ight is still 1.7x faster and 6.9x more energy-efficient, using photonic tensor core (PTC) calls as a normalized energy proxy.
check: Full text (Sec 4.1-4.2, Fig 10) supports every number. Quotes: "Prior protocols can only handle toy models (2,000 params) given their algorithmic inefficiency and instability, while our L2ight shows >1,000x higher scalability to handle large ONNs (10 M)". Also: "Though MixedTrn achieves comparable accuracy to L2ight on small benchmarks, we are still 1.7x faster and 6.9x more energy efficient." The comparison baselines are FLOPS [DAC 2020] and MixedTrn, both zeroth-order (ZO). Energy proxy: "Our simulator counts the total number of PTC calls as the normalized energy indicator". In Fig 10, the 10M point is C100/Res18. The pipeline is IC (calibration), then PM (parallel mapping of the pretrained model, analytic plus ZO), then SL (in-situ subspace learning with multi-level sparsity: feedback, column and data sampling). All results are software simulation with noise models; there is no real chip. Note: the abstract's "over 30x better efficiency" is measured against prior sparse-training methods (RAD, SWAT-U), not against FLOPS/MixedTrain.
relevance: Strong counter-evidence: perturbative/zeroth-order learning loses badly even on a physical substrate where it is the 'natural' in-situ method. The winning recipe reuses a pretrained model and a gradient-based subspace update. C2's chances shrink unless it is scoped to small or adaptation layers. The paper also shows that sparsity inside on-chip training has already been explored.

title: On-Device Fine-Tuning via Backprop-Free Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Prabodh Katti, Houssem Sifaou, Sangwoo Park, Bipin Rajendran, Osvaldo Simeone
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG; v1 2025-11-14, v2 2026-05-05; comment: "Conference submission; Under review")
claim: Gives a theoretical estimate of the relative model sizes that fit in on-device memory under BP (stored activations and optimizer state, only partly relieved by checkpointing) versus memory-efficient zeroth-order optimization (MeZO, forward passes only). It then shows numerically that MeZO has accuracy advantages for on-device fine-tuning under memory constraints, provided enough wall-clock time is available.
check: The abstract (arXiv API) matches the claim: "provides a theoretical estimate of the relative model sizes that can be accommodated under BP and MeZO training... MeZO exhibits accuracy advantages under on-device memory constraints, provided sufficient wall-clock time." The full text (pdftotext of v2) says "MeZO can accommodate models at least 2x larger than BP within the same budget", rising to up to 25x at long context, and about 5x with checkpointing.
relevance: This counters the project's equal-memory GPU result, where memory-saving BP beat forward gradient and NP: the opposite conclusion is published for the fine-tuning regime. It suggests the honest positive result for perturbative learners lies in adapting a pretrained network (low effective dimension), not in from-scratch class-incremental training. Any 'BP wins at equal memory' claim therefore needs a scope. The same group's arXiv:2608.21223 (implicit-perturbation zeroth-order training on IMC, 16 nm energy model, 0.46-0.83x the perturbation energy of explicit weight perturbation) appears in the tool notes but is missing from the paper table.

title: Loihi: A Neuromorphic Manycore Processor with On-Chip Learning
authors: Mike Davies, Narayan Srinivasa, Tsung-Han Lin, et al. (23 authors per Crossref)
venue: IEEE Micro 38(1):82-99
claim: Loihi (60 mm^2, Intel 14 nm) integrates programmable synaptic learning rules on chip; its LASSO solver beats CPU solvers by over three orders of magnitude in energy-delay product. Later papers cite it for Loihi's learning cost of 120 pJ per synaptic update, taking 6.1 ns (Communications Engineering 2023, doi:10.1038/s44172-023-00117-9, ref. 51). A 2023 memristor learning engine reports 10.61 pJ per STDP update as 11.31x below Loihi (doi:10.1109/tbcas.2023.3291021), which is consistent with about 120 pJ. The paper itself is closed access and was not read; the number comes from these two secondary citations.
check: The abstract (OpenAlex) supports the 60 mm^2 / 14 nm / programmable synaptic learning rules claim and the LASSO claim: "over three orders of magnitude superior energy-delay-product compared to conventional solvers running on a CPU iso-process/voltage/area." The secondary citations were checked directly. Comms Eng 2023 (s44172-023-00117-9) says "Loihi by Intel has a system level consumption of 120 pJ energy per synaptic update, which required 6.1 ns [51]", and its ref 51 is Davies et al., IEEE Micro 38, 82-99 (2018). The TBCAS 2023 abstract gives 10.61 pJ STDP and an 11.31x reduction compared with Loihi, and 10.61 x 11.31 = 120.0 pJ, which is consistent.
relevance: This fills a gap the neuromorphic scout named: no public per-update energy, so any per-update cost would have to be assumed. A C4 scoreboard built on the SANA-FE Loihi preset can use the published figure of about 120 pJ per synaptic update, a design figure rather than a measurement, instead of an undeclared assumption. It is also the seminal on-chip-learning chip paper a reviewer will expect; the list has only the 2021 Loihi survey.

title: Activity dependent structural plasticity in neuromorphic systems
authors: Richard George, Giacomo Indiveri, Stefano Vassanelli
venue: 2017 IEEE Biomedical Circuits and Systems Conference (BioCAS), October 2017
claim: In neuromorphic analog VLSI the number of synapse circuits is the binding limit on scalability. The paper proposes a runtime structural-plasticity mechanism that allocates this limited synapse pool, using neuronal activity to pick the event sources that best drive each postsynaptic neuron, so as to make optimal use of the on-chip resources.
check: The abstract supports the claim: "We propose a mechanism that allocates the limited number of synapses during runtime, in order to choose event-sources that best contribute to the postsynaptic neurons activity." It also names the synapse-circuit count as a scalability limit of neuromorphic analog VLSI, and says activity serves as an indicator for "making optimal allocation of the resources". The abstract says nothing about per-neuron budgets that scale with activity.
relevance: This predates C4's core idea of activity-dependent allocation of a fixed synapse budget on a neuromorphic chip; the neuromorphic scout reported no hardware precedent. C4's novelty has to narrow to activity-proportional per-neuron budgets (hub allocation), combined with a class-incremental stream and NeuroBench-style costs.

title: A Simple Rule for Dendritic Spine and Axonal Bouton Formation Can Account for Cortical Reorganization after Focal Retinal Lesions
authors: Markus Butz, Arjen van Ooyen
venue: PLoS Computational Biology (PMCID PMC3794906)
claim: Homeostatic structural plasticity: a neuron creates new spines and boutons when its electrical activity is below a homeostatic set point and removes them when its activity exceeds that set point. Spine and bouton formation depends only on the neuron's own activity. This rule reproduces cortical reorganization after focal retinal lesions. The neuromorphic tool notes say NEST's homeostatic structural plasticity follows this model.
check: Europe PMC abstract: "a neuron creates new spines and boutons when its level of electrical activity is below a homeostatic set-point and decreases the number ... when its activity exceeds this set-point." Also: "Spine and bouton formation depends solely on the neuron's own activity level." The abstract reports that the rule reproduces visual-cortex reorganization after focal retinal lesions (spine turnover, bouton overshoot then pruning, retinotopic remapping). The claim is supported.
relevance: The standard brain-derived rule for per-neuron connection budgets runs in the opposite direction to hub allocation, which gives budgets proportional to activity: here over-active neurons lose inputs. A reviewer will ask in what sense hub allocation is 'brain-like'. C1 and C4 should include the homeostatic (inverse-activity) budget as a control and justify the sign.

title: Analog Physical Systems Can Exhibit Double Descent
authors: Sam Dillavou, Jason W. Rocks, Jacob F. Wycoff, Andrea J. Liu, Douglas J. Durian
venue: arXiv preprint (cond-mat.dis-nn, cs.LG), v1 21 Nov 2025
claim: The authors demonstrate double descent on a physical Contrastive Local Learning Network: 32 self-adjusting transistor edges in a resistive network that trains itself with no digital processor. The task is 2D binary classification with 7% of labels flipped. Network size is fixed at P=32. The authors sweep the number of training points M from 1 to 64, so the x-axis is P/M; they never vary edge count. The peak appears only in test hinge loss, at P/M ≈ 5.3–6.4; test classification error is monotonic. Standard coupled-learning training shows no peak. A modified clamping protocol ("overclamping"), which tolerates component non-idealities, does produce it. The authors suggest that biological systems might also benefit from over-parameterization. Consequence for C3: this is indirect evidence. The paper does not show that adding or removing edges changes generalization. Using it against edge pruning is an extrapolation. It is still a reasonable reason to report test loss (including a margin or hinge loss, not only accuracy) across the parameter/data ratio.
check: The metadata is correct, and the abstract supports the summarized content. Full text: "Our networks are fixed in size and therefore parameter count, so to study double descent we vary the number of training data points." The hardware is a CLLN with 32 self-adjusting transistor edges and 16 nodes. The modified protocol is "overclamping". The double-descent peak appears only in the test hinge loss, peaking at P/M = 32/5. Test classification error is monotonic in P/M. Without overclamping, no peak appears (Appendix C). The over-parameterization point is phrased as "suggest that biological systems might similarly benefit from over-parameterization".
relevance: This is counter-evidence for C3's subtractive premise. In the very substrate C3 targets, adding edges improves generalization, so removing edges during learning can land on the interpolation peak. C3 must report test accuracy against edge count along the whole double-descent curve, not only power and training fit.

title: Frequency Propagation: Multimechanism Learning in Nonlinear Physical Networks (arXiv v1 title: "Frequency propagation: Multi-mechanism learning in nonlinear physical networks")
authors: Vidyesh Rao Anisetti, Ananth Kandala, Benjamin Scellier, J. M. Schwarz
venue: arXiv preprint 2022 (cond-mat.dis-nn), published in Neural Computation 36(4), MIT Press, 2024
claim: In a nonlinear resistive network with variable resistors, an activation current is applied at the input nodes at one frequency and an error current at the output nodes at another, at the same time. Each conductance is updated in proportion to the product of the two frequency-demodulated local coefficients. The rule is local and proven to perform gradient descent, and the paper frames it as 'multi-mechanism learning' that covers electrical, elastic and flow networks.
check: The abstract (arXiv and Crossref) supports the claim: "an activation current is applied at a set of input nodes at one frequency, and an error current ... at another frequency." It also says "Each conductance is updated proportionally to the product of the two coefficients. The learning rule is local and proved to perform gradient descent." The paper calls this multi-mechanism learning for "resistive, elastic, or flow networks". The response is described as a superposition of the two signals, so they are present at the same time with no separate free/nudged phases.
relevance: This is the closest precedent found for C5: inference and error signals coexist in one physical network, with no separate free and nudged phases. It can be implemented directly in the resistor-network simulator recommended for C3. C5's novelty therefore reduces to the pruning component, and frequency propagation belongs next to EP and coupled learning as a baseline.

title: Self-learning Machines based on Hamiltonian Echo Backpropagation
authors: Victor Lopez-Pastor, Florian Marquardt
venue: arXiv 2021 (first version 2021-03-08); published in Physical Review X 13, 031020 (2023)
claim: Gives a general scheme for autonomous self-learning in any time-reversible Hamiltonian system: the parameter updates happen autonomously, with no external processing and no need to know or control the internal parameters. It is demonstrated numerically on coupled nonlinear wave fields. A 2025 follow-up (arXiv:2506.06248) derives Hamiltonian Echo Learning as a special case of Lagrangian EP and notes that it is forward-only, local, and needs only two or more passes through the system regardless of model size.
check: The abstract supports the claim: "neither external processing and feedback nor knowledge of (and control of) these internal degrees of freedom is required... general scheme for self-learning in any time-reversible Hamiltonian system", demonstrated numerically on "coupled nonlinear wave fields". The follow-up arXiv:2506.06248 (Pourcel, Basu, Ernoult, Gilra, 2025) is real, and its abstract says HEL (including HEB) is derived as a special case of GLEP and is "forward-only... requiring only two or more passes through the system regardless of model size, and enables local learning."
relevance: This counters the view that local rules win on physical substrates while backprop belongs to GPUs: gradient learning can itself be native to physics. A physical-substrate scoreboard for C3 and C5 should include physical BP-like methods as baselines (Hamiltonian echo methods, in-situ photonic BP), not only digital BP.

title: Training Deep Boltzmann Networks with Sparse Ising Machines
authors: Shaila Niazi, Navid Anjum Aadit, Masoud Mohseni, Shuvro Chowdhury, Yao Qin, Kerem Y. Camsari
venue: arXiv preprint 2023-03-19; published in Nature Electronics, 2024 (Crossref date 2024-06-17)
claim: Sparse, asynchronous, massively parallel p-bit Ising machines on FPGAs train deep Boltzmann networks in a hybrid probabilistic-classical loop. They use full MNIST and Fashion-MNIST and a reduced CIFAR-10, with hardware-aware sparse topologies. On MNIST, about 30,000 parameters (4,264 p-bits) match the 90% accuracy of a software RBM with about 3.25M parameters, and only the sparse network can also generate digits. The machine runs a measured 50-64 billion flips/s, at least an order of magnitude faster than GPU/TPU implementations, and handles CD-n with up to 10 million sweeps per update.
check: Every claimed number appears in the abstract and full text. Abstract: "our machine using only 4,264 nodes (p-bits) and about 30,000 parameters achieves the same classification accuracy (90%) as an optimized software-based ... RBM with approximately 3.25 million parameters".
